speechtext: Consideration of the motion of Mr. Alfred Thompson for an address to His Royal Highness the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Wednesday, January 20.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned last night I had just finished presenting to the House a few words in connection with matters which had been brought up during the course of this debate, and I was about to refer to some things which had been lengthily discussed by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Car-vell). That hon. member has seen fit to discuss at very great length in this House a question which, from my point of view, and I think from the point of view of a good many other people, it was not in the public interest to discuss. On that point I shall speak a little later. I shall not attempt to follow the ramifications of my hon. friend's arguments, because it would be very hard to follow them, even should I desire to do so; neither shall I attempt to follow all the reckless statements that he made in connection with the subject. I sometimes think that democracy, for whose existence we are fighting now, and coupled with democracy the love of freedom and the liberty of free speech, is not an unmixed blessing when the privilege of freedom of speech degenerates as it sometimes does into license. My hon. friend has made a good many reckless speeches in the course of his career in this House; and he has got into trouble a good many times in this House; he would have got into trouble a good many more times outside the House if he had said outside the House what he has said inside the House. I might, in that connection, direct my hon. friend's attention to the excellent editorial in the Ottawa Free Press of last night, in which the editor cordially invites my hon. friend to repeat the remarks made here in reference to the Free Press outside of this House, when he will find himseslf in the law courts.
Would my hon. friend pardon me.
Order.
Have I made a misstatement?

I just want-

I want to inform my
hon, friend that I have written a letter to the Free Press, and I am going to give them all the opportunity to bring all the actions they want in the courts of law.

I am perfectly sure that the House is exceedingly interested in that, and I would suggest that if my hon. friend is very hard pressed he can secure the distinguished legal services of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley).
And he will win for me, too.

My hon. friend, in the very long speech which he made the other day, started out with .a misstatement of fact. Of course that is not very surprising, although it is rather astonishing to hear a gentleman who is always so keenly desirous of' bringing down proof for every statement he makes, starting out on an argument with an absolute misstatement of fact. In starting to discuss the question of hay in New Brunswick, he made the statement that the conhnaotars in 1915, the Atlantic Hay Company, had 'a contract, for
7.000	tons of hay which was increased later to 10,000 tons. My hon. friend, if he is going to make statements of that kind, should try and get somewhere near the truth because that contract of 7,000 tons was never increased to 10,000 tons. And he makes the -statement further on in that speech, that after they -had filled the terms of this contract they immediately went after more, and he broadly intimates that they got more. I am here to s-ay that they never bad any other contract than that for 7,000 tons. A little further on, he states that the contract was given for $24 a ton for compressed hay; and then -at page 263 Hansard he says:
These men were given a contract for 7,000 tons of hay, afterwards increased to about
10.000	tons-
I have shown the inaccuracy of that.

am not sure; I was-
I thought my hon. friend was always so sure of the facts.
-under the impression that the contract price was $24.50. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs knows about this, because he and I talked the matter over.

Mr. Carvell: That was one night last spring.
Mr. Reid:	You are referring to something
which took place a year ago.
Mr. Carvel1.: I am referring to something which took place a year ago.
An hon. Member: That is too deep for him.
Mr. Carvell: No, it is not too deep for him. The Minister of Customs and I will not quarrel over the matter. If he had been allowed to handle this thing there would not have been the terrible condition of affairs that exists in New Brunswick to-day. The Minister of Customs told me' that the contract price was $24.50.
There was never a contract given for $24.50. There was no mention of it, .and the Minister of Customs could never have said it. My hon. friend the member for Carleton should not have believed it, because he did not get the facts, and he could have got them if he had wanted to. I shall not go into the whole question of that contract, but I wish to touch on some features of it. It was given on January 4, 1915. I did not happen to be here at the time, because I was then recovering from pneumonia and was in the Southern States. The department, however, and those who had anything to do with the department, acted in perfectly good faith in giving that contract. My hon. friend refers in very scathing tones to the iniquities-he almost used that phrase-of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who, he gives us to understand, is playing havoc with everything that is good and pure and righteous in New Brunswick, and whom he holds responsible for these things. Well, if a matter came up concerning the province of New Brunswick, I do not know that it would be a crime to ask the advice of, or to consult with, the minister who represents that province in the Government. If my hon. friend ever achieves the distinction- I do not think it likely that he will-of being a cabinet minister, I can easily believe that he of all men-
You know that some very ordinary men have become cabinet ministers.

If my hon. friend ever
did achieve such a distinction, he would be the first to expect to be consulted when things come up in connection with his own province. I do not think my hon. friend is ever likely to achieve that distinction; looking at his record, I certainly do not think he ever will. The hon. member for Carleton was elected in 1904 by a majority of 274. He appealed to the electors again in 1908, and he had meanwhile forfeited their confidence to the extent that he got
in by a majority of only 154. He appealed again in 1911, to find that he had forfeited nearly all the confidence of the electors because he hnly got a majority of 11; that time he got elected by the skin of his teeth, and if he continues to keep up his reputation in this House he will certainly not get elected next time. I think it would be good policy on the part of my hon. friend to support an extension of the term of the present Parliament, otherwise we may not see much more of him.

used in caucus?
Now let me refer for a moment or two to the question of hay. The first offer we had of pressed hay was from Kennealy and Wetmore. I think they are Conservatives

No, Liberals; one, of
them is anyway.

I am not sure about
their politics. Anyway, on January 2, 1915, they made an offer of 10,000 tons of hay at $21.50 a ton. The condition was made that the Department of Agriculture should furnish the presses and the tender was not accepted. I think, perhaps, it would be well in that connection to put two letters on Hansard, because they will show how the thing took place.
St. John, N.B., Jan. 2, 1915.
J. A. Ruddick, Esq.,
Commissioner, Department of Agriculture, [DOT] Ottawa.
Dear sir,

At the request of Hon. J. D. Hazen we have submitted a tender for ten thousand tons compressed hay delivered West St. John for War Office account.
Hon. Mr. Hazen advises us that your department can arrange for the presses for this business. Will you advise us full particulars of the arrangements covering this item so that we may take the . necessary steps to complete arrangements providing our tender is accepted.
Awaiting your reply, we are,
Yours very truly,
Kennealy & Wetmore, Ltd.
Messrs. Kennealy & Wetmore, Ltd.,
St. John, N.B.
Dear sirs,-I have your letter of the 2nd instant, which has crossed mine of the same date. I do not know what the Honourable Mr. Hazen had in mind when he advised you that this department could arrange for compressors to handle New Brunswick hay. As a matter of fact the only presses which the department has control of at the present time are those which are in use at Montreal. There must be some, misunderstanding on that point.
Yours truly,
J. A. Ruddick,
Commissioner.



These letters explain why at that time Keunealy & Wetmore did not get that contract. The Atlantic Hay Co. was the only other tender received or considered at that time, and a gentleman came down here-I am now only speaking from memory of what Mr. Ruddick said, because I was not here at the time,-I think he was the son of a member of the firm, or at all events he was some one connected with the firm. The matter was discussed, and he asked for a contract at the price of $24, at which price they offered to supply their own presses. My hon. friend knows that the cost of . freight, and of the installation of presses and motors comes to a very considerable sum; they put it at about $20,000.

Thirty cents a ton will
pay for the whole thing; 1 did it.
Will my hon. friend sit down.
I will keep the hon. gentleman straight.

May I speak to a point of order, Mr. Speaker; we "may as well get the air cleared before we start on this subject. I would not object to any hon. gentleman opposite asking the privilege to correct a statement of fact. I hope I would not object to that; I have never objected to it, and no man would object. But I do object to be constantly interrupted if the interruption does not relate to any question of fact. The interruption of my hon. friend had nothing to do with the statement I made. I simply referred to the cost of the presses; I am not referring to the cost of the pressing at all. I made the plain statement that this firm stated that the presses cost them nearly $20,000 to purchase, to freight, to install and to operate the motors.
I deny that; that is not true.
I think my hon. friend should correct his statement. The words " not true " are certainly not parliamentary.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I say it is not a correct statement of fact as to the cost of these presses; that is all.

I am amazed at my hon. friend who is a lawyer, being so absolutely out of his province, and showing such a lack of intelligence. I did not say it was a fact; I stated that the gentleman who came here claimed that the cost was $20,000.
Tt is a wonder they did not say $40,000.	.
Just keep quiet. Let me tell my hon. friend that he will get all he wants before I am through.

I must ask hon. members not to interrupt the hon. minister. I understand he desires to have the protection of Rule 23, which every hon. member is entitled to when addressing the House. I ask hon. members not to interrupt the hon. member.
All right.

Now, I can elucidate this point which we were discussing perhaps a little more clearly. I made the statement that the contractors who ,came up here considered that it cost them nearly $20,000 to install those four presses, with their equipment. My hon. friend says that is not a fact, if I said it, but I did not say it. I do say that it comes pretty nearly to that sum, and I am going to give the best proof I can for that statement. It is a fact that my hon. friend himself when he had a contract with the Government in 1902 put in a certain claim for loss after finishing his contract, and in that claim he stated that the amount invested in his pressing plant, consisting of two presses, was $8,530. That comes pretty close to it.
That is not $20,000 for one press.

to be worse, I had the bales put back and re-j -ole-1 same.
I have the honour to be sir,
Tours truly,
(Sgd.) J. L Cooke.
This is a letter to Mr. Ruddiok from Thos. C. Strong:
Dear Sir,-I feel it my duty to let you know what is being done in regard to the Kennealy & Wetmore contract-
I am dealing now with the general question of the class of hay which was accepted, and with my hon. friend's charge that black, rotten hay went to the War Office, a thing which would certainly distress me as much as it would him, if it were a fact:
-I feel it my duty to let you know what is being- done in regard to the Kennealy & Wet-more contract.
These parties are buying all the cull hay that I sorted out of two thousand tons and are shipping it to St. John and having it compressed there, so you can take whatever actiop in the matter you see fit.
Tours respectfully,
(Sgd.)Thos. C. Strong.
Then here is a telegram from Mr. Rud-dick to Mr. Cooke:
Inspector Strong, Woodstock, reports Kennealy & Wetmore shipping all hay rejected by him to West St. John. Look out for it.
With respect to this transaction, I may tell the House that this hay was watched very carefully and that little, if any, hay, that should not have gone did actually go. The best proof that such is the fact is that Messrs Kennealy & Wetmore say that they could not fill their contract owing to the heavy rejections. They say:
Owing to heavy rejections it is possible we may be short about thousand tons; we have more hay on track than presses are handling; we are not delaying them; may possibly be able to complete in Montreal.
Both Kennealy & Wetmore, and Stevenson, who also shipped hay to Montreal, had a large amount rejected, and, as I have stated that Kennealy & Wetmore were absolutely unable to fill their contracts because they could not get the hay owing to the heavy rejections. I have referred to the Stevenson contract. As he could not get the amount of hay he wanted in time, he shipped to Montreal and very much of the poor hay was rejected and he was therefore put in a similar position. Certainly there were a lot of difficulties about these 1915 contracts. The point I want to make is this: It is quite possible that, looking back, it would have been better to have paid the contractors, who certainly had a very hard 
row to hoe a little more and the Atlantic Hay Company a little less. But the whole transaction was conducted in absolutely good faith by those who were here while I was absent and statements made about the exorbitant profits of the company are absolutely beside the mark. The best proof that the hay was not of the character that my hon. friend described it to be is that we had not a single complaint about the hay from the War Office when it arrived in France and they were absolutely satisfied with it. We furnished the War Office with all the accounts and details that they wanted in regard to these transactions and no complaint whatever was made. In the earlier stages of large undertakings of this kind which are suddenly thrust upon a department, it would be astonishing if mistakes and blunders were not made. Does my hon' friend think that any department of the Government in times such as these can suddenly take hold of a transaction of this kind and make no mistake whatever? I do not profess to toe infallible, neither do the officers of the department; but we all endeavour to make as 'few mistakes as possible, and in absolute good faith to rectify those mistakes which may have been made in the past. Let me point out to my hon. friend, that the War Office, having had a full account of all these transactions up to that time placed before them, not only did not say: we find no fault in you in connection with these transactions, but since that time they have placed on my shoulders increased responsibilities in connection with supplies for the armies at the front.
I come now to the transactions of this year, with which I am ;a little more familiar. This is a story which I think will interest, if it does- not weary the House, for my hon. friend has dealt with it pretty vigorously already. A contract was given to the Atlantic Hay Company this year for 15,000 tons at $23 a ton. This contract was for hay, compressed from eighty to one hundred cubic feet to the ton, and which would pass inspection at St. John. This company owned four presses. We thought that it was not at all likely-and I think my hon. friend will admit this-that there would be as much hay available in New Brunswick this year as last. We thought, and rightly so, that it would be more convenient for us to deal with the one firm owning the four presses. I think there was only one other press in the whole province able to do that work. Furthermore, we thought it would

be better for the War Office we should have our inspection at one point, and at the price of $23 a ton it would be giving the hay to the War Office at $2 less a ton than was being paid for Montreal hay, adding freight, to St. John.
Is it not a fact that the four presses now used by the Atlantic Hay Company were not at that time in the province of New Brunswick but in Montreal?

I did not say they
were in New Brunswick. I said that the Atlantic Hay Company owned them, and that they were available-

No. Mr. McDonald
owns them.

Mr. McDonald is, and
has been, a member of the Atlantic Hay Company. We thought that in giving this contract we should not only be ensuring to the War Office a good class of hay at a * reasonable price, but that the contractors would also be able to give a fair price to the farmers, and not make any undue profit for themselves. We believed in good faith, that it was a contract that could be entirely justified. Other offers came in soon afterwards, and I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend from Carleton, who thinks that we do everything for Conservatives and nothing for anybody else, that several of these offers came from strong Conservatives and were not considered for the reasons I have mentioned.
I know it. [DOT]

Subsequently the honourable member for Carleton started in the press a great controversy on hay matters generally in the province of New Brunswick. My hon. friend cherishes a very poor opinion of the contractor, Mr- B. F. Smith. I am not very familiar with New Brunswick politics-I know they are very vigorous-but I think that Mr. Smith may have been my hon. friend's political opponent, or is going to be. Anyway, my hon. friend cherishes an exceedingly mean opinion of Mr. Smith, judging from what I have seen of the controversy, and I am quite sure Mr. Smith cherishes an equally poor opinion of my hon. friend opposite. When I was ill with the grippe a little while ago, the hon. member for Carleton came to Ottawa to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was at that time acting premier, and who, as an old citizen of New Brunswick,
knew conditions in that province fairly well, I suppose. My hon. friend from Carleton set forth a great many statements in regard to this hay controversy in New Brunswick, and produced a dazzling array of figures as to cost of pressing, freight, shrinkages, and various other things, to such an extent that he made out that an iniquitous state of affairs existed, and that the farmers were not getting a look in. He demanded, in very vigorous tones, 1 should gather, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should immediately compel those rascals down there to give to the farmer two more dollars, or whatever it was, or that another) contract should be let, or that the embargo which had been imposed should be lifted. I may say that the embargo does not affect New Brunswick to anything like the same extent that it affects Quebec, inasmuch as during the whole four months since the last hay crop and prior to the imposing of the embargo, only 400 or 420 tons were shipped from New Brunswick to the United States. My hon. friend made all these statements, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as he naturally would under the circumstances, that if such a state of affairs existed it was deplorable, and that he would turn the matter over to the Minister of Agriculture. He said he would have Mr. Ruddick come over and discuss the matter with him, and if everything was as the hon. member for Carleton had stated, something ought to be done to remedy it- In that visit-and I am not breaking any confidence in saying this -my hon. friend from Carleton mentioned that he himself would benefit to the tune of several hundred dollars if the farmers got a bigger price; I presume he has several hundred tons of hay himself. He said to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as he has in effect said to me since in a letter: Give this extra money to the farmers, make these people pay more, or let the work out to other contractors, or lift the embargo; and if you will do one of these things I will not say a thing about it.
That is all true.

He -was going to get a bigger price for the farmer, for his friends and for himself. I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend that in everything connected with this hay business I have been only too glad to consult with the Minister of Trade and Commerce on every step that 1 have taken, and on the correspondence, and anything that has been done in that

matter since my hon. friend visited the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been with the entire concurrence of my colleague. Among other things that my hon. friend discussed with the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time was that we should give to Mr. McCain, a friend of my hon. friend opposite, a contract for three, or four, or five thousand tons of hay in that part of New Brunswick where my hon. friend lives, and that this would settle it. Subsequently Mr. McCain wrote to the department; he had written once before. In one case he wrote offering to take a contract for from three to five thousand tons at $22.50 a ton. He could well do that. In any case it would not have been much better than what we were doing, even if other circumstances had been equal. We should have had to send a spe'cial inspector up there, and more expense would have been involved in pressing the hay at Woodstock. Mr. McCain subsequently made an offer of $23 a ton and pay $15 to the farmers. He could well do that. The Minister of Trade 'and Commence, who knows the fact, observed that it might 'be possible in one small district where there was a considerable quantity of hay and conditions were more favourable in regard to labour, and freights not so much -as in other parts' of the province, to get the hay for less than we could at St. John; but he pointed out that that would interfere with the general arrangement for the whole province. That point was well recognized, because as my hon. friend has stated, when Mr. McCain got a contract in 1902 there was a considerable difference in the price, viz.-$14 f.o.b. Florenceville, as against $17 St. John. We therefore did not consider it advisable to take that step, nor did I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce consider it advisable. Subsequent to the visit of my hon. friend, Mr. Smith came to Ottawa. He also went into this hay question and put up a lot of facts and figures and I think was able to show that some of the statements of the hon. member for Car-leton might be questioned as regards expenses of operation and various other details. At all events, he made the statement-and there may have been some force in it- that they were getting only a reasonable price for their hay contract and that he was willing to pay and would pay what he considered a fair price. That price might fluctuate from time to time to the farmers, and he did not expect to make an unreasonable profit; but as so much had been said about it, and as Mr. Smith 
and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) had been scrapping and fighting so [DOT] hard and filling the newspapers of St. John and other parts of New Brunswick with this controversy, Mr. Smith offered to transfer his contract to any other firm in New Brunswick, under exactly the same conditions, and allowing the department to fix a reasonable price by arbitration for the expenditure he had incurred and for the expenses of his plant. Now, that was a pretty fair offer. We did not accept that offer, nor did we accept another offer that he made, for very sufficient reasons. In the first place, it would have been inadvisable, from the department's point of view, even if the offer had been accepted, to transfer the contract, because it would have meant delay in the delivery pf hay and in the adjustment which would have been necessary under the conditions of the transfer. Mr. Smith also made another offer to which I am now going to allude. It is strange, however, during all this time that the controversy was going on and under the dismal state of affairs as pictured by the hon. member for Carleton, that neither the department nor I, myself, received a single protest from any farmer in New Brunswick in reference to this matter, and the only protest that I ever heard of at all came through one letter that was sent, I think, by the hon. member for Carleton to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), and which is not now in my possession, because I returned it, and the letter which my hon. friend read' in the House. The letter to which my hon. friend referred was from a Mr. Fawcett, whom I do not know at all. My hon. friend referred to him in most eulogistic terms, and I recall, in the opening phrase of Mr. Fawcett's letter which he addressed to Mr. Carvell at Woodstock, that he looked upon Mr. Carvell as the one man in New Brunswick who would give agriculture a square deal, and that it was a matter of great thankfulness that they had such a man in the country. It would not be very difficult to infer that he is of the same affiliation as my hon. friend.
There is no doubt about that at all. He is a good Grit, if there ever was one.

The point I make is
that not once had there been any protest to the department, or to myself, or any explanation or suggestion, and I am informed from other sources that on the

whole the New Brunswick farmers have been fairly well satisfied with the condition of things. However, I was not going to leave the matter there, and I did not leave it there. I went into the matter again and discussed it thoroughly. I asserted to Mr. Smith, what I have always asserted from the start and what I asserted in a letter to my hon. friend, namely: that the sole object the department has as a trustee for the British War Office in this matter is to help as far as we can to get a market for the Canadian farmer, and while getting him a fair price for his product-and he would get a much fairer price in this way throughout the country than he would have got if the War Office had not stepped in- at the same time to get the War Office a good article at a reasonable price, and to ensure that the contractors do not make an unreasonable profit. On that occasion, or subsequently, Mr. Smith wrote me this letter, which, with my reply, I wish to place upon Hansard:
Ottawa, 10th January, 1916. The Hon. Martin Burrell,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-On my return to New Brunswick from a trip to the cities of Ontario and Quebec I found that the number of reckless, absurd and indeed silly assertions which had been bandied about in the public press and otherwise, in regard to the contract of this company to supply hay to the Department of Agriculture, had been indeed larger and their character more gross than I was aware of at the time of my recent visit to your department.
On that occasion and on January 3 following, as an evidence of the good faith of this company, 1 submitted two alternative propositions. One addressed both to the department and the public was as follows:
"We, the Atlantic Hay Company of St. John, New Brunswick, are willing to transfer our hay contract with the Department of Agriculture to any firm in New Brunswick who will agree to deliver the quantity of hay to the department, and carry out the terms of the contract; provided such firm or person arranges to pay us for expenses incurred to the date of the transfer and takes over for use our plant at St. John, the figures to be paid for the use of plant and for disbursements incurred to be determined by arbitration under the direction of the Department of Agriculture."
The other was made direct to your department and reads of follows:
"We, the Atlantic Hay Company of St. John, N.B., agree to cancel our contract with the Department of Agriculture (Dominion) and buy and compress their hay in the war bale on the basis of 5 per cent for handling the entire output of the province available for that purpose during the season, all books and vouchers to be open at all times to the department and a final audit made under the direction of them. Price to be paid the farmer and for hay delivered at West St. John to be fixed from time to time by the department."
I have explained why we did not think it advisable to consider the first offer, and I thought that it was not advisable to accept the second one, because, after I had consulted with the department, it did not seem clear that there would be any induce- _ ment to keep down the expenses of operation. The letter goes on:
As a further evidence, however, of the determination of the company to deal absolutely fairly both with the farmers and the department, and to show that the contract as originally made is based on that principle, we now make this additional voluntary offer:
We are ready to submit to the Department of Agriculture all purchase vouchers, books, documents and papers relating to the carrying out of the contract. The department may determine the sum which may be fairly allowed for all expenses connected with the purchase of said hay, freight, the operation of compressing plant and otherwise incidental to the final delivery of the compressed hay, and having so determined we agree that if the' department finds there is any profit to our company beyond one dollar (51.00) per ton, such excess profit will be retained by, the department for the benefit of the Imperial Government.
I will be glad to hear from you at once as to the above.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) B. P. Smith, for the Atlantic Hay Company.
To that letter I replied:
Ottawa, Ont. Jan. 11, 1916.
B. P. Smith, Esq.,
The Atlantic Hay Company,
East Florenceville, N.B.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your letter and note what you say in reference to the controversy which has taken place about your hay contract.
There was certainly no intention on the department's part when this contract was given that it would permit any exorbitant profits to be made. Our desire was that the War Office should be supplied with hay at a reasonable price, that the farmers should get an opportunity of disposing of their product at fair figures, and at the same time the contractor should not reap undue profits.
You have made several suggestions, but I think that the one contained in your letter of the 10th, namely, that you are willing to undertake that your profits shall not succeed $1 a ton, and that the department itself shall fix upon a proper basis for the expenses, is very fair and affords strong evidence of your good faith in the whole matter, and I shall therefore be glad to act upon it.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) M. Burrell.
My hon. friend might say, perhaps, that it would be very hard to determine that.
Impossible. You do not know whom you are up against.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is not a point of order, and the hon. member knows perfectly well that it is not.

I am going to discuss this episode pretty thoroughly, and I am going to keep myself within the bounds of the rules of this House, but I am going to set forth the facts so that there cannot be any mistake. My hon. friend and myself may -have some difference of view as to what was confidential and what was not. So far as the whole matter that took place is concerned, it would not hurt me very much if anybody had been there to take it all down, and reproduce it in the public press. As to the contract, I did say, perhaps, that that was confidential, hut it scarcely mattered beeasue. I had given the hon. gentleman the assurance in that very letter that I had ample safeguards. But this is what I am complaining of. I understood he did not want me to refer ,to this thing unless he took it up; but it seemed to me an extraordinary thing to try to tie my hands and rob me of any defence in this, when I had already been stabbed in the back by these other statements he had made. I want to say to my hon. friend, and nobody knows this better than he, that I never used the phrase " In God's name do not bring this up;" that I never said it would be bad in the newspapers, because there is nothing that I have ever done in this Parliament that I would be ashamed to put in every newspaper in the country. Talk about being amazed! I never was more amazed in my life than when the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) used the phrase de did. I cannot understand any man doing such a thing. To my mind it is the most deplorable incident that has ever taken place in this House, since I have known it. My hon. friend may laugh, it does not do him credit; that is all I can say about it.
What did you say?

I do not know what his own view of these matters is, but if he has this interpretation of what is an honourable

course to take-I say nothing about my hon. friend's conduct or character or anything else in his private life-but if that is his interpretation of what can be done in public life, nothing can stamp him so well as being absolutely unfitted for public life as that one thing. I think I can comment on this, and show the absolute grotesqueness and absurdity of my hon. friend's contention. I went to the Prime Minister soon after I got. my hon. friend's letter telling me that he had the power of speech, and intimating, as I thought, and rightly thought, that he was going to bring all hay matters in connection with the War Office up in this House, and I stated to the Prime Minister my views on the matter, as I did to the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster). My views were these; that we were operating in a very large way for the War Office, on account, of the military forces, all over this country, purchasing hay, oats and flour. When the whole story comes to be written, when the war is over, it will be only too great a pleasure for me to bring down the whole details to the country, for it is a great work, a very much larger work than anybody imagines. But no business man in this House can come to any other conclusion than that it is inadvisable to bring up these matters in Parliament when the war is on and these supplies are being contracted for, and large operations are going on in all these businesses all over the country. It does not matter so much in his own newspapers down there; they would not attach the same importance to any remarks the hon. member for Carleton might make as they would to his remarks in the House where he gets a fictitious importance by virtue of being a member of this House, and to give it publicity for that reason, from my point of view, was not in the best interests of the War Office or of the public. At all events, I stated that view to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They understood it was not in the public interest, and they will bear out what I say. I said it did not matter to me personally whether it was brought up or not, that I had, I thought, a sufficient answer to anything that might be said; but that, solely and entirely on account of the public interest and the War Office interest, I thought it not advisable to discuss this in the House. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce agreed, and I suggested, and they concurred, that I should speak to my hon. friend and put that view 
before him. In fact, the Minister oi Trade and Commerce suggested that I could appeal to my hon- friend's patriotism in this matter, and it was suggested, by either myself or the Prime Minister, that, if I liked, I could speak to the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on this broad line. I was very glad to do it for this reason also, that on the 7th of April, 1902 a gemitleman in this House, who has now passed away, the late lamented Hon. F. D. Monk, placed a question on the Order Paper asking for partiicula/rs about the purchase of ihay for the War Office during the South African war; and Mr. Speaker, the then Minister of Agriculture gave this answer, which I think was an absolutely correct and proper answer to give:
This question, relating- entirely to the business of the Imperial War Office, I am not at liberty to answer it.
I think that was a perfectly proper answer, and not a man on our side disputed its justness. In 1903 the matter came up again in the shape of an Order asked for on the floor of the House by the Hon. Mr. Monk, for all this information, because the war was then over. A long debate took place, which was referred to by the hon. Solicitor General the other night. We asked for all correspondence, documents, papers, etc., all the particulars about the transactions, of people like my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) who then had a contract with the Government for the War Office-The debate was participated in by my right hon. friend, by Mr. Fielding, by the late Postmaster General and others. We took the ground that, as the war was over, it was perfectly proper to bring down all these matters, as they did, to some extent, concern the people of Canada. I am not dis^ puting whether they were right or wrong, but the late Government took the ground, very emphatically, that, as it related to the War Office and it was Imperial money which was spent here, it was not a responsibility incurred to this House, and they did not think it right to bring the information down, and they did not bring it down. They put it to a vote and the motion was negatived and the Order was not granted. I am not disputing whether the position of the late Government in 1903 was right or not; I say it was absolutely right in 1902 but in 1903 it might be open to question; and I say right here and now, that after the war is over, speaking for myself, and I think the Prime Minister

would feel the same way, I would have absolutely no hesitation in bringing down every single record we have got in connection with these transactions.
At all events, I took the course which I have outlined, a course which was suggested or concurred in by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not know whether 1 am counted as a very strict party man. Sometimes I think that some of my friends who are strong party men do not so regard me.
I am a good Conservative; I think I have a right to stick up for Conservative principles and Conservative practice, however deplorable that may be to gentlemen like the hon. member for Carleton. I have a great many friends in my own constituency on the Liberal side. I have many Liberal friends in Ottawa-some of my warmest friends are Liberals in politics. I hope 1 have some friends in this House who are Liberals in politics and sit on the other side. I never held the doctrine that one should carry one's political animosities into private life, nor would I regard life as being tolerable if I had to do it. I want to say this further in regard to this matter with which we are dealing, that I would rather go out of public life forever, and walk out now, and keep such regard as I may have been fortunate enough to get from any of my friends as a public man, than remain in public life at the price of descending to the depths to which my hon. friend for Carleton, N.B., has descended. It may be said thfit that is not a matter of very great public interest; but I do appeal to you, and to the older members of this House who have sat here for many years, that this is the sort of thing that touches the finer side of life, and makes public life tolerable. And iso it is well worth touching when we are dealing with this matter. I have already spoken of the grotesqueness of my hon. friend's assertion that I said " for God's *sake don't bring the matter up in the House; the papers will get it, and how bad that will be." I have already said that there was absolutely no truth in that assertion. 'I never used such words at all; I did not refer to the newspapers, nor did I use the name of God at all in any shape or form, so that my hon. friend does not know where he is at. If I feared anything; if my hon. friend was so absurd as to. think I was afraid that there might be public exposure, why I had an easy way out; I could have done what the member for Carleton demanded, and' got out of
the mess, if mess there was. But of course I was not in any way afraid, 'because I had nothing to conceal. I was simply speaking in the public interest. Now I do not like to bring the names of other people into this matter, and I will apologise to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition for mentioning his name in connection with it. I would not have done so if it had not been for what the hon. member who sits behind him (Mr. Carvell) said. He not only made the absolutely inaccurate statement I have referred to; he intimated-he did not say so in so many words-that I had gone running to the leader of the Opposition and to the Liberal Whip for the same reason, that I was afraid of this thing coming up in the House.
My hon. friend made the statement first; I did not.
I spoke to the hon. member for Carleton, and he refused to promise that he would not speak on it.
That is right.

I was actuated absolutely and solely by the view that this matter affected or might affect the War Office and the public interest. I said I did not t.bink it would be advisable in the interests of the War Office to do so, but that if he did, he must do it according to his own judgment. I met the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee) in the corridor, I think a .few days afterwards. I told the Liberal Whip that I would like to speak to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition in regard to the matter, as I thought it of sufficient public importance to place my views before him, as the Prime Minister had Suggested. My right hon. friend was busy at the time, and I could not get access to him. I told Mr. Pardee, the chief Liberal Whip, the circumstances in exactly the same way, namely, that I did not think it advisable in the interests of the War Office to bring this matter up, 'but that my hon. friend from Carleton seemed determined to do so, and if he did, all. right. I said that I would reply and would be able to refute anything he might say that seemed to reflect on the department or bn myself. Subsequently I was enabled to see my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and I was treated by him with the courtesy which he has always shown to me since I came here in 1908 as a back bencher from the far western province. I am appealing

to him in a sense; it is an appeal to Caesar from one of Caesar's very insignificant legionaries. I know my right hon. friend will bear me out that it was precisely in this tone that I placed the circumstances before him. I simply said I did not think that a discussion of this matter would be in the best interests of the War Office, that we had not made any of our proceedings public, that we did not think it desirable to do so, and that I thought the contract sufficiently safeguarded the public interest.
I said, I am not in a position to implore you to insist that Mr. Carvell shall not speak; I simply put this to you, and if he does speak, well, all right I ask again, I ask any man in this House if my attitude has not been absolutely consistent throughout this whole matter, and I leave it to the judgment of the House to say whether what has been done, in order, I presume-for there could be no other object in view-to secure some little political capital by having it repeated in the press, that I begged somebody to call him off. Is this fair? I ask what sort of fighting in the House of Commons of Canada in this year of grace, 1916, that is!
I say that if ever there was in this House an exhibition of hitting below the belt that was it. My hon. friend expressed pity for me the other day. He said he was sorry , from the bottom of his heart for the poor Minister of Agriculture, who had fallen an innocent victim to the wiles and machinations of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen); that I was a very decent chap and so forth. What sort of man is this that can violate the code of ethics which is prized by those who cherish the good old name of gentleman?
Now, Sir, much as I hate the tu quoque argument; much as I dislike saying that the other fellow has been doing things, therefore pitch into him; I think it only right to ask who this man is who brings these charges and makes those wild and reckless assertions. Who is this gentleman who has such a disinterested and passionate zeal to secure better prices for the farmers in New Brunswick and for my hon. friend's friends. Who is he? Well, I noticed the other night that he was a little uneasy. He seemed to think that I would probably speak after him, and he was quite right. He used these words:
X know what kind of defence my hon. friend is going to put up; he is going to say that in 1902 when I had a small contract,
and so on. My hon. friend was beginning 
to get uneasy, and was afraid I might say something that would hurt. On page 265 of Hansard he says this:
I have had experience in this matter. During the South African war I was a member of a company that compressed hay, and I speak with knowledge. I was not then a member of the legislature or of the House of Commons,
I was a member of the New Brunswick Hay Company.
My hon. friend was secretary and treasurer, the whole body and bones of the institution; at all events he was the most prominent man in it, and the man who appeared here to do all the business with the department. He added, " We had a small contract from the Department of Agriculture, about $7,000 altogether."
Mr. CARVELL,: Seven thousand tons, not dollars.
It is $7,000 in Hansard, but I accept my hon. friend's correction. He says it was a small contract. My hon. friend had contracts altogether amounting ' to about 11,000 tons.
Not filled.

Pretty nearly all filled; we have the records, and they show that they came pretty nearly to 11,000 tons, which, figured up at the price he got, which was $17, came to about $187,000; not very small. Now, my hon. friend at that time got a price of $17 a ton for compressed hay at West St. John; he will correct me if I am wrong in any of my statements. My hon. friend anticipated that I would deal with this or would say something about it. He pointed out that they were giving the farmer at that time $8 a ton, and he thought what an exceedingly good price that was, considering what hay was at that time. In fact, he went the length of saying-I could give the exact figures, and I shall come to them presently. They were giving the farmers $8 a ton.
I want to point out one or two things. My hon. friend has contended that under ' this contract, at $23 a ton, the spread between the price obtained by the farmer for his loose hay and the price that the contractor gets for his compressed hay, which passes inspection, is a tremendous one, and that the contractor is going to make the enormous profit of two or three dollars a ton-three dollars, was it?-or, at all events, a very enormous profit. Under a contract like this it would amount to some $45,000. The contractors, unquestionably, in different parts of the province of New

Brunswick, pay different prices. We have never insisted on fixing a price, but we have insisted that he shall give a fair price. He has given as high as $13.75. I have had that information in most positive terms. My hon. friend admitted that he had given $13.50. I will take my hon. friend's lower figure of $13.50, which gives a spread of $9.50 between the loose hay of the farmer and the compressed hay supplied to the Government. But my horn, friend says that at that he makes a tremendous profit. There was a spread when my hon. friend had a contract of $9. I do not think that my hon. friend will dispute that the cost of operation in 1902 was lower than it is to-day.
I dispute it.

My hon. friend disputes it. When I make a statement of fact my hon. friend feels it incumbent upon himself to dispute it. He had four hours in which to speak, and I do not think he can begrudge me another half hour. I do not think any business man would doubt that the cost of operation would be heavier today than it was in 1902. My hon. friend has made the statement that it cost more because they had to compress to a limit of 70 cubic feet to the ton at that time, and we are now compressing to a limit of from 80 to 100 cubic feet to the ton. We have compressed a good deal to 80 cubic feet. My hon. friend did not compress all of this hay to 70 cubic feet; there was much of it that was compressed to a less degree than that.
Have you any record of that?

At all events, this is a small matter, because I am informed by those who know what they are talking about in the department, that the difference in the cost of compression as between 70 and 80 feet would be absolutely trifling, and that they would use less wire with the tighter compression than with the other. When my hon. friend says that these people, with a contract at $23 a ton, are imposing on the farmer, and that I am filching out of the pockets of the farmer and holding up the War Office and everybody else for the sake of enabling these contractors to amass filthy lucre, how does it compare with the amount that he himse f made when he had the contract? What are the facts? So far. from his having amassed a fortune out of the business in 1902, when
the war closed, he came back on the department with a claim for $13,000. I must in fairness say that no doubt his was a harder position, because, the war having closed, it left a certain amount of hay on his hands. But that was not included within the terms of his contract. He came back upon the department with a claim for $13,435 to compensate him for loss under his contract, because the termination of the war left him with a considerable amount of hay on his hands. A Liberal Government was then in power, the department was presided over by Mr. Sydney Fisher, but he could not stand for the rapacity of my hon. friend, and he turned him down and would not give him the amount that ;he asked for.
He is a patriot.

Yes, he is a kind of patriot. I do not like saying these things,
I hate saying them, but I think it is time the House should know the type of man who is making these reckless charges. In regard to the price paid, my hon. friend, at.page 272 of Hansard said this:
Among the men in that arrangement were Mr. Smith, Mr. McCain, and a dozen other hay merchants in the county and in the three or four adjoining counties. Prior to that time hay had never been worth more than $6 a ton, loose in the farmer's barns.
He qualified that by adding that it had not been worth more than $6 or $6.50 a ton. I am not a New Brunswicker, but I am informed by a New Brunswick man that for ia long time the price had been from $6 to $10 a ton for loose hay in the farmers' barns and I cannot believe that there is any province where the maximum price of loose hay to the farmer in his bam would-be only $6. I have farmed myself for a good many years and it would be a discouraging business if all that a man could get for loose hay in his bam, after paying the expensA of cultivating, seeding and harvesting, was $6 a ton. If that is my hon. friend's experience I do not wonder that he is looking like a very unhappy type of farmer. My hon. friend introduced this argument-or so it looks to me-because he evidently knew that I wis going to allude to the price which he had to pay at that time. He goes on to refer to the fact that he had to pay $8, but I have been informed that at the time my hon. friend's contract was in force, and when he was performing it, he brought hay in from Quebec which assisted in regulating the price. If my

hon. friend denies it I will accept his statement that he did not bring any hay in from Quebec.
My recollection is that we 'brought in about ten cars of hay.

I am glad to know that because it fixes the price at $8 and if my hon. friend brought in hay from Quebec it looks like a very judicious way of keeping the farmer in New Brunswick satisfied at not getting more than that. Further on my hon. friend says, in regard to this $8 a ton, that they bought hay from sub-contractors and that the sub-contractors among themselves made an arrangement by which they would pay $8 a ton to the farmer. The House will gather, and 1 think everybody will gather, from that suggestion, that $8 was a reasonable price .and that my hon. friend, who had a large contract, and who was to supply 11,000 tons to this Government, with a spread of $9 between the price that he paid for loose hay and the price which he received for compressed hay, should make something substantial out of his contract; whereas the fact is that it landed him in the hole to the extent of $13,000 according to his own showing. But, at all events, they were .paying the farmers only $8. My hon. friend made the contracts with the sub-contractors and, 'by the irony of fate, one of the sub-contractors was the very firm which has the contract mow that my hon. friend is denouncing in this House. I have a copy of the contract which my hon. friend drew up in regard to the sub-contractors. My hon. friend said, you will recall, that the sub-contractors made an arrangement amongst themselves by which they would pay the farmers $8 .a ton. I want you to listen to some of the phrases. I take it for granted that, as my hon. friend was the sec'y-treasurer of this company, a gentleman who had been very active in coming up and getting contracts made with the Government and in presenting the claims, he would have everything to do with the framing of the sub-contracts.	.
I presume that, being an astute lawyer, he would not adopt any cheap police court methods, or have any junior law students around, but would do the work himself because of his knowledge of the law and out of his born zeal for the farmer. He says we are bleeding the farmers. Inflamed with that splendid passion of patriotism, of a local kind, and sympathizing with these unfortunate men, he of course would do the 
right thing. Let us see what was put in this contract.

and so on. It continues:
The said Company, in consideration of this contract hereby agree that they will not pay any other person or persons whatsoever, a greater amount for hay, during the continuance of this contract, than the sum of ten dollars and twenty-five cents,-**
That is for baled hay.
-as aforesaid, f.o.b., nor 'will they allow Mathias Meagher, William A. Estey, Coles W. Dugan, Harris Everett, George A. Davis, H. H. McCain, Bohan B:-os., Charles E. The hon. member for Carleton came down here and demanded that I fix the price and fix it high, or he would expose me in this House by his power of speech; but here we see in this contract these men were not allowed to pay more than $8 to the farmer. Let us read on a little further, and my legal friends who understand legal phraseology will of course be better able to appreciate this than a simple farmer like myself:
And in case any of the said parties shall, during the continuance of this contract, pay! or offer to pay any farmer in the county of Carleton a greater sum that eight dollars, then they agree, upon satisfactory proof of such paying or offering to pay, to refuse to purchase or receive any hay from the said offending

-from the said , offending party or parties, and also, that in case Bohan Bros, shall pay or offer to pay to any farmer in the counties of Carleton or Victoria, excepting that por-

t'on of the parish of Kent lying north of Bath Station and east of the River St. John, more than eight dollars for their loose hay, as aforesaid, then, upon satisfactory proof of such payment or offering of payment, the Company agree to pay the said A. C. Smith & Company for the remainder of their contract then unfulfilled, whatever amount the said Bohan Bros., shall have offered or paid above eight dollars in excess of the ten dollars and twenty-five cents.
I do not know New Brunswick geography or politics very well, but I understand that Bohan Bros, were doing business in a small section where there was a great hive of votes, all of them the right way, and therefore they could pay a little more. But I am not insisting upon that, I do not want to be unfair to my hon. friend. Here is another interesting clause:
It is also agreed that neither of the above parties shall be at liberty to pay for hay already pressed to any farmer more than nine dollars and twenty-five cents per ton, under the same penalties hereinbefore mentioned as in the case of an offer of more than eight dollars for loose hay.
It is also agreed between the parties hereto, and made a condition hereof, that in case the said A. C. Smith & Company, or any of their recognized agents or representatives in the counties of Carleton or Victoria, shall be known to have paid or offered to pay to any farmer a greater sum than eight dollars for loose hay

My hon. friend even gave credit to these notorious people for having some bowels of compassion and thought that out of the kindness of their hearts they might possibly pay a little more in some cases. So he says that if they pay more than eight dollars for loose hay-
-that for the balance of the contract then unfulfilled they shall deduct the sum of twenty-five cents per ton, excepting in the case where trades have been legally concluded prior to the date hereof, and in the case of the other parties above mentioned who are buying hay for the said Company shall bona-fide, prior to the date hereof, have made legal trades for hay in excess of eight dollars, then-
-then the punishment hereinbefore provided.
Mr. Speaker, you can hardly wonder at my asking what sort of a patriot this is. He says I am bleeding the farmers, this gentleman who binds them down hard and fast says that these contractors shall be punished if they pay the farmers more than eight dollars. It continues:
Then the punishment hereinbefore provided shall not apply in such case, and also, that in the case of any of the parties purchasing hay for the Company as aforesaid, shall be known hereafter to pay or offer to pay any farmer more than eight dollars for his hay, excepting in the case above mentioned where a bona-fide trade has previously been concluded, then upon proof of such paying or offering to pay.
there shall be the sum of twenty-five cents per ton deducted on all hay not actually paid for up to that date.
In plain language the contractor is not allowed to pay more than eight dollars to the farmer; apd if this contractor, who now is the Government contractor and upon whom I am imposing no strong conditions except that he shall not get more than $1 a ton profit, should under this agreement I have in my hands pay $8.40 to the farmers, say on two thousand tons, then he would be find $500 for doing it. All that I have to say on this matter has been said. I think it is a pretty sordid sort of tale and I do not want to touch on it any further. I have, I think, made a fair presentation of the department's point of view, and in disposing of this hay matter I repeat that the country owes a debt of gratitude to the officials of the department, who, night and day, in season and out of season, without an extra cent of pay, have for over a year tried to do the square thing by the country and by the War Office. As far as I am concerned I have been animated by no other motive. I have nothing to conceal, and I am willing to be judged on this whole matter by the speech I have made in the House here to-day. I do not want to discuss the matter further.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have not mucn more to add, and have indeed already taken up too much time; but in connection with such matters as have been discussed here during the last few days, I would like to point out that in the multifarious and complicated situations that war brings, especially to those democratic nations who are not organized for war, the constant pressure, the necessity of large and hasty industrial adjustments, place almost impossible burdens on the shoulders of governments. No government under such circumstances can avoid blunders and mistakes. The British Government is not immune, nor is it likely that the Government of a young country like this, which never had a thought of war in its heart before this outbreak occurred, could be^the millennium is not yet come.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who is not in his seat, referred to the heavy additional obligations that were placed on ministers. He made a graceful reference to the Prime Minister, and unquestionably this House and this country will recognize that never since Confederation has so heavy a load been placed on one man's shoulders as upon his, and they will also bear testimony that that burden has been borne and those duties discharged with unflagging devotion and conspicuous

ability. We shall agree also with the hon. membex for Pictou in his reference to the heavy additional work on the Minister of Militia, whose tremendous energy has been an inspiration in these trying days. To the Minister of Finance also such a tribute is due. Ministers holding that portfolio do not always get the full recognition that they might, possibly because the work involved does not make so obvious and forcible an appeal to the public as in other cases. But in the case of my hon. friend who now occupies that high office, (Sir Thomas White), we all abundantly recognize the tribute which the country owes to him for steering with such consummate ability the financial ship of state through the present troubled waters: The hon. member for Pictou thought other ministers did not have much to do. I suppose we can let that pass, though he probably did not intend that that should be taken very seriously. But I would like to add that not only in the case of ministers holding portfolios, but in the case of the three members of the Government without portfolios, and I refer to the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), to Senator Lougheed and to Sir George Perley, each one is doing as earnest, self-sacrificing and useful work as any of the members of the Administration.
I think it is due also to those very many departmental officers upon whom heavy burdens have been imposed, that a tribute should be paid to the spirit in which they are doing their bit, not minding much heavy and extra work and much longer hours than in times of peace.
What all countries want in such times is that their governments should earnestly strive night and day to prosecute this war to a successful conclusion, and if they do these mistakes and blunders will be forgiven, and in any case such mistakes and blunders will be judged by the people at the conclusion of the war.
There is a worse thing, however, than making mistakes, and that is to have a mind poisoned by the desire continually to criticise and carp, not for constructive but for destructive purposes. It was satirically said of the Republican party in the United States prior to the last election, that it was a party consecrated to keep in office. If it is bad to be consecrated to keep in office, it is equally bad to be consecrated to the task of trying to get into office.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has made a speech of between four and five hours in this House. He made a 
brief ten minutes' reference to the war. The whole of the rest of his time was taken up in a reckless discussion of scandals, or alleged scandals. I presume he is patriotic enough to want to win this war; but if one were to judge merely by the length of time that he has given to the respective subjects, one would be almost justified in saying that he was far more anxious to smash this Government than he was to smash the Germans. He spoke of the pain caused him by having to speak of all these dreadful things, and shed crocodile tears while suffering the acute distress of a manufactured anguish. The hon. member for Carleton has no doubt heard of Pecksniff, and I will refer him to a fresh study of his great prototype.
In view, however, of all that he has said and of my own already too long remarks, if he is inspired with any sense of manliness, he might well regret and deplore having made such reckless and baseless assertions as he did in this House on Tuesday evening last. I again apologise to the House, not only for taking the time, but for dealing with this subject as I have had to do. It is a task that I have hated and loathed. I am quite sure-and in this I am sure I shall have the concurrence of my hon. friend the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), who takes the larger view- that the country is sick of this intercalumniation at tins'time. There are bigger things and more vital things filling the thoughts and minds of the people, and I would not have touched on this subject had it not been forced upon me by the hon. member for Carleton.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in his remarks in reference to the shadow of this great war in -which we are all resting, said that the shadow was even greater at the present time than when this House last met. I trust this is not so, and that, trying as the present condition of things is, there may be much behind the scenes that makes for a speedier and happier turn of events than we think. Not one of us can or must doubt the final achievement of victory, and to that event all our thoughts and energies should be turned.
There are very many other important questions that should be touched on in a time like this, some that my hon. friend from Pictou touched on in the close of his speech-questions of great importance to Canada after the war, such as land settlement, educational work, etc. It is the business of the Government, not only to

think of all these things, but to welcome the criticism and the suggestions of all our friends opposite, and of other people in the country who have helpful criticisms and suggestions to make, in order to enable us to do something more, something bigger in the way of constructive work for the country which we love.

But I do propose, in the discharge of my duties as a member of the Opposition, to offer some criticism of the Government before I take rriy seat. This, under ordinary circumstances, would be the last session of this Parliament. Hon. gentlemen opposite would naturally go before the electors and tell them what they have done as nation builders in laying the foundation for future wealth in this country, because wealth will not come through inertia. What has the Government done for the future prosperity, for the future wealth of this country? The Government has done absolutely nothing except to rely upon the patience of the Canadian people in increasing by every means possible their taxes; and upon the credit of the country in effecting loans to cover, in great part, their extravagant expenditure, which to-day is a by word throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion. The best service we can do to the people of Canada at the present moment is to keep the keenest watch upon the way that the people's money is spent and to watch these blunders and this extravagance that the Minister of Agriculture informed us this Government was liable to on account of the war. The people have willingly and patriotically given their

assent to. the levying of the funds necessary to carry on Canada's share in this worldwide war; but the people will hold their representatives responsible for any failure in controlling or condemning looting and speculation in the administration. The people of Canada fully realize that the members of the Opposition have gone far in supporting the Government in their war measures and will go further; but the people of Canada must also realize that in the expenditure of that money not even my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), whose whole life has been one of unselfish and unswerving devotion to Canada and to the Empire, has been consulted. What is our position in Canada? We are borrowing; we are taxing the people of Canada. The Government informs us, through the Minister of Finance, that it is absolutely necessary to raise money by way of borrowing and by way of taxation. We have been told that there are two ways to meet the Canadian financial situation. The Minister of Finance, in a very able address in the city of Toronto before the Board of Trade, dealing with that particular subject of how we shall face the financial situation, used these words:
Well, I am old-fashioned. I do not know any other way for Canada to become a lending country and to save more money than to produce more and save more. The hon. What is our condition in Canada? I do not think I could put it better than it was put in the Toronto Globe some time ago, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote from the Globe. The article is ' entitled-I beg the Government's pardon for giving the title-" Have spent money like a drunken sailor."
As the people of Canada begin to understand that the heavy burden of the new taxation' is not imposed to pay the Dominion's war bill, but to meet a huge deficit in the ordinary expenditure of the country, a feeling of amaze ment spreads throughout all classes of the community.
The ordinary expenditure during the last four years of the Laurier government was, in 1908, $76,641,000; 1909, $84,064,000; 1910, $79,411,000 ; 1911 $87,740,000. The Borden government came in during October, 1911, and became responsible for the expenditures of the year ending March, 1912, which were $98,161,000. These expenditures were based in some measure on Mr. Fielding's figures, so that responsability may be said to rest on both parties for 1912. In 1913 the expenditure on consolidated revenue account went up $112,059,000, in 1914 to $127,384,000, and for the current year ending March 31, 1915, Mr. White says it will be $140,000,000. For the year ending March, 1916, he estimates that it will be the same amount.
Now what does this mean to the taxpayer? Setting aside all war expenditures and all expenditures on capital account, the Borden government, less than four years in office, has increased the cost of operating the ordinary services of the country and of paying interest on the country's debt from $87,774,000 to $140,000,000. Assuming that there are now eight and a half million people in Canada, this means additional expenditure of $6.14 for every man, woman and child in the Dominion.
In the year ending March, 1911, the country's revenue from taxes was $89,835,000. In 1914 it was $127,478,000. In the current year ending March 31 there will be a great falling-off in customs revenue, and as a result an enormous increase in the public debt. In the year ending March, 1916, the people of Canada will have to contribute in taxes at least $140,000,000 if they are to pay their ordinary current expenditure, apart entirely from the cost of the war.
The government of Canada has been spending money like a drunken sailor, and now the people must pay for the debauch. They will have to keep on paying long after the present generation has ceased to bother about taxes. The year the Laurier government came into power the interest on the public debt was $10,645,000. When it went out fifteen years afterwards it was $12,535,000. Mr. White tells us that in the year ending March, 1916, it will be $21,000,000. Before such figures is it to be wondered at that the country stands amazed?
Now what is the solution which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance offers in regard to that situation? He says: "borrow money and raise taxes," and I suppose he implies that our income will increase, and that we must live on that income. His

words, uttered in this House at the last session of Parliament, were:
It is therefore the intention of the Government to negotiate for a continuance of the arrangement which I have mentioned with the Imperial Government for the purpose of procuring the funds necessary to meet our spec.ul war expenditure. . .
It is not a question of raising a few millions by stamp taxes, by income tax or other minor means of supplementing revenue. We must endeavour to raise additional revenue to an amount of at least thirty million dollars, and when we have accomplished this we shall still be obliged to borrow heavily over the next fourteen months, that is to say, between now and March 31, 1916, to meet expenditure for purposes other than for war.
I have a very great respect, I may say, for the Minister of Finance, and I fully realize the difficult position in which he has been placed since the beginning of the war. I sympathize with him, perhaps, on account of the very humiliating position in which the Government placed him when they sent him to New York to borrow $45,000,000. I have not very strong feelings as to where we get the money, provided we get it; as to where we get our trade, provided we have it; as to where we sell our goods, provided we sell them. But, just prior to the election of 1911 I had almost become-how shall I put it?-I had almost become convinced after listening to the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite, and who were then in Opposition (my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was not among them at that time, that is why I presume he was chosen to go to New York) that we must have no trade or truck with the American people. Up to that time I had thought the Americans were a very fine people. I make a point of visiting the United States at least once a year, and there are some things in their institutions one cannot yet admire; yet there are many things to admire, and one is the great progress the United States has made commercially and financially. Hon. gentlemen opposite told us that it was disloyal to have any trade or truck with the American people. I did not much believe in this lip-loyalty, but in my own humble and modest way I did want to be loyal to the institutions of my country, and of the Empire. Hon. gentlemen opposite said it was disloyal to deal with the American people, but how much more disloyal must it be to go begging to the American people for money to carry on the business of this country. The day I saw the Minister of Finance starting down to the station to buy his ticket for New York, carrying that carpet handbag which had been'bequeathed to him by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce 
-the same carpet bag which my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce had used in his former trips to Washington-I felt that his position was a painful one, and I have wondered how he explained it to the American people. I suppose he said: "I was not in the House at the time they were saying it would be disloyal to trade with you; I need money now; I have become converted to other ideas;
I will pay a higher rate of interest than any one else; will you lend us a little? I congratulated him when I saw him come back with $45,000,000 in his pocket. He will be back again. I put this question to my hon. friends opposite: What are you going to say to youx loyal constituents that you deceived the people? Prior to 1911 you taught them that we must have no trade or truck with the people of the United States. What did the Finance Minister do with that $45,000,000? He told us, in his Budgot speech last year, that he required the money to fill the gap between revenue and expenditure. Here are his words:
It is obv'ous upon consideration of the figures which I have submitted that we shall not, by any reasonable supplemental taxation measures, be able to close the gap between revenue and expenditure, much less to pay a portion of the principal of our special war outlays.
But, what about those taxes imposed in the Inland Revenue Department? What about the increased postage on our letters? How did we get that deficit in the Post Office Department this year of some $3,000,000? Where has the money gone that was received for the stamps? We pointed out that the stamps would go to pay no part of the war expenditures, but the minister assured the country that not only had they to impose special taxation but they had to go and beg of the American people to loan them $45,000,000 to fill the gap between the revenue and their expenditure. Now, Sir, may I be permitted to offer a word of advice to the Government at this moment? The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) says we must live within our revenue. I can conceive the scene around the Treasury Board when my hon. friend repeated that advice to his colleagues, and when he said to them: We are practically financially bankrupt; you have been spending, according to the Toronto Globe, like a drunken sailor. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) says: We need the money, we have to give the boys the buildings they want. The Minister of

Finance says: I cannot possibly give you any more money; I have not got it. The Minister of Public Works says: We must have that money. His friends upon the other side of the House insisted upon getting the luxuries to which they were accustomed before the war. Then what did the Minister of Finance do? He appealed to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden)-he will correct me if I am wrong-and said to him: Can you not help me to control my colleagues? They are accustomed to all the luxuries; we had heaps of money when we came into office because the country was prosperous and the Liberal Government had left the coffers full, but we have spent the money and we have no more. The Prime Minister shrugged his shoulders, looked more bothered than usual and said: What can I do; I am not the Finance Minister? The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) apparently needed more money to purchase hay. These hon. gentlemen around the treasury board called out as one man: Mr. White, take up your carpet bag and go back and get more money from the American people. But he said: I cannot go back to the American people; it is too humiliating a position. Where will you go? they asked. He said: I will go to the Canadian people, and he went to the Canadian people and borrowed more money. What does Sir Edward Walker, President of the Bank of Commerce and chief financial adviser to the Borden Government, say about all this borrowing? I am not objecting to the borrowing of money for war purposes; I do not wish to be misunderstood.
