In thus urging the Government to be careful how they face the problems of the future,
1 want to tell them that, whilst the farmers of this country have much to fear through the actions, or lack of action, of the present Government, the manufacturers of this country certainly also have very much to fear because this Government is so tiding them at the present moment to increase this output in the way of war munitions, whilst at the same time following out the main plank in the policy of the Conservative party, as I think every hon. gentleman opposite will admit, whilst following out their theory of offering every possible protection to manufacturers in the way of an increase in the customs duties. In order to prove what I have just advanced relative to the ccondition of our manufactures owing to the war, I want to quote an item which I find in the Labour Gazette, a newspaper published by this Government:
Exceptionally active conditions prevailed throughout the year in the large iron and steel works at Sydney and Sydney Mines, and also in similar industries in Quebec and Ontario. Practically all foundry and machine shops in the country were .busy in the manufacture of munitions, and large orders for cottons, woollens, clothing, leather and other goods used in military equipment kept establishments handling these lines in the main industrial centres of the Dominion very busy. The steel plant at Sault Ste. Marie was also very active during the year.
We therefore have it announced in this mouthpiece of the Government, the very reason why we have an increase in the export of manufactured goods. The Minister of Finance, I know, will agree that the increased exportation of agricultural products is entirely due to the war, so that this year is not a year upon which my hon. friends opposite can claim to have found a new system by which they have lessened this

adverse balance of trade against Canada. They must of necessity appeal to normal conditions, to the conditions which existed in this country prior to the war, in 1911, 1912, 1913 and 1914; and I claim that the Government has signally failed in that respect to meet the conditions which confront Canada. The Financial Post of Toronto, of January 22, had a very significant article entitled, " Business outlook after the war.'' I will not quote the whole of the article, but for the purposes of my argument I read:
Whether or not in the readjustment Canadian manufacturers will be able to obtain business to replace in volume that of making war materials is a problem which the future can best solve, but it would appear conclusive that Canada's best hope will be large agricultural products. Along this line the directors of the Banque d'Hochelaga emphasize the necessity for increased population to offset the lowering of prices when the war ends. The report, after advising caution on the grounds that the present war prosperity is not healthy nor likely to be permanent, continues :
The annual report of the Banque d' Hochelaga contains this statement:
" One may assume that, at the end of the war, Europe impoverished and weakened, anxious to recover and to get back its economic situation, will endeavour firstly to provision itselftin greater measure at home, and then at prices' as advantageous as possible. It will therefore be necessary for us to see to it that we regain by increased production what is lost through the lowering of prices. To this end, the increase in our population by the colonization of our vast territories, the improvement in methods of agriculture and a special attention on the part of our farmers to the raising of live stock must remain from a material point of view, our greatest natural aim."
When I say, Sir, that it is the duty of the Government to show the people of tips country that they have some policy in view by which they hope to meet conditions after the war, I am simply asking the Government, in the name of the people whom I represent, and of a good many people in this country, to give an indication of how they expect to meet the conditions the moment war ceases.
I shall refer for a moment to the Shell Committee, which has been prominently discussed during this debate, and in that connection I do not intend to make allusion to any particular person, or persons. We have heard it -said that there is a general demand for an investigation into the operations of the defunct Shell Committee. That demand has come from hon. members in this House, and apparently the feeling is general throughout Canada.
It is not confined to those of the political

. faith to which I belong; it has also come from Conservative sources. My hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) quoted from the Electrical News in the course of his speech, and I shall cite from the same paper, an article written by a gentleman who said he preferred the Borden Government with all its fault to the Liberal Administration. The article says:
The Shell Committee was appointed by the Government, was representative of the lortrn-ment and consequently representative of Canada. In so far as our dealings with the British Munitions Board is concerned that committee was Canada. And in this great war, which Lloyd George has said is a war of munitions rather than men, shall it be said that when the Empire, called for 'aid, when the brave men in the trenches shouted for munitions, Canada rushed to their aid with $1 worth of shell in one hand while the other was held out for $5.15? Shall it be said that while we ere wont to twit the United Statesers witn their fondness for the dollar our own country has outdone them in the hour of the Empire's peril? It is unjust that Canada should be allowed to rest under any such stigna; it is unjust that the manufacturing members of the Shell Committee should be retired under suspicion of having placed such stigna on their native land. In justice to those men and to justice to Canada the shell contracts and the Shell Committee should be given the fullest and most searching investigation.
Yesterday the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, acting upon his responsibility as a member of this House, brought very serious charges against the Shell. Committee. These charges were of such a nature that, it seems to me, the Government, for its own honour, to preserve its dignity, and for the honour and dignity of the people of Canada, should at once grant an investigation. I .am not always governed by what appears in newspapers, Grit or Tory, but the Montreal Star, which professes to be a strong adherent of this Government, and which has been a very staunch supporter of my hon. friends opposite, on the 26th of this month, editorially used this language:
It must be increasingly apparent to every well-wisher of the Government that a public and complete investigation into tn>
wc-k of the late Shell Committee and other wvr purchases cannot be denied. If the consent of the British War omce must be secured to legaliz; such an inquiry, then it should be asked for by a unanimous Canadian Parliament. Too much has been charged to enable public opinion in this country-deadly in earnest as it is in its determination to win the war-to sit down in patient ignorance as to the real facts of the case.
The charges are far too serious-cn s questions at issue far too vital. The finest young men in Canada are giving their lives to defend the Empire and the fixed principles of lib [DOT]. fy and honour for which it stands before humanity and history. If, while these noble young men

have been going out of our homes to die " somewhere in France " ghouls in human shape have emerged from homes of similar outward appearance next-door to pad their pocket books with unfair and unearned profits on the arming and equipping of these young men, then +he whole country wants to know it-and to know them- and to know what the Government proposes to do to them.
Every dollar taken unfairly from the money which this nation has to spend in self-defence, is like striking up a rifle aimed at a German. Worse still, it may even be disarming a Canadian lad in the face of a German charge. The whole business must be searched through and through with the vivid light of patriotism and publicity. If the moneys we are literally sweating out of ourselves to save freedom and the flag, are being diverted into traitorous pockets, then there are far worse Germans in Canada than those whom we have interned. .
That is very strong language, but it is not as strong as that which was used by the Right Hon. Lloyd George, who, speaking in , the British House of Commons last July, said that on account of the very high prices demanded for war munitions in some quarters, delay was caused and in consequence a great deal of sacrifice resulted on the battlefield in France. Where are those quarters? Is Canada one of the quarters to which Mr. Lloyd George referred? The Canadian people are asking that question to-day. What is the reason that is prompting the Canadian Government to refuse this investigation? The Minister of Militia, discussing this subject yesterday, spoke very bravely, according to his view, when he said:
For a double reason, therefore, I do not see that t is the function of this House specially to inquire into any of the transactions in connect o i with that committee-
That is a question that I will come to in a moment.
-although I should be more than pleased, so far as I am able, to give all the elucidation of the facts, and all the enlightenment as to them which it is possible for me to give.
Hon. gentlemen opposite will say, and I thoroughly agree with them, that the Minister of Militia is a man of such mettle as to stand up in $his House and say in effect:
I am one man in this Cabinet and I will give all the information I have. Then, I ask the other members of the Cabinet: Why is it you do not hold an investigation and give the Minister of Militia a chance to give to the people of Canada all the information which he has in his possession? The only answer given so far is the answer given by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). The Solicitor General is a very keen reasoner; he has a very nimble political conscience, and, he satisfied himself and apparently satisfied the leader of the Government when he said: The Shell Committee is a creature of the Imperial Government; the Shell Committee is responsible to the Imperial Government; the Shell Committee communicates directly with the Imperial Government, and therefore, this Government has absolutely no jurisdiction over it. Has this Parliament no jurisdiction over the actions of the Shell Committee which was dealing with persons and property in this country? Have you ever heard of any man in Canada who could state a fallacy better than the Soiicior General and build up an argument upon it just as if it were a truism? He said he was not going to speak for the Shell Committee, although he made as able a defence of it as he knew how, but that he was going to speak in the name of the Government and give the reasons why there should be no investigation. He started out by saying:
I do not know that it is a matter that requires much elucidation that the prices should at first have been higher in Canada than in the United States. It may be that the prices were higher than the conditions warranted; I am not an expert, and I do not know.
Mr. Lloyd George, on the other hand, said in the British House of Commons that on account of the prices being higher there was some sacrifice on the part of the Allied armies. This is, of course, a matter of indifference to the Solicitor General because it has nothing to do with the legal phase of the case. He proceeds to say:
I have said that I have no knowledge that he (the Minister of Militia) was a member, and I would like my hon. friend to get the names of the respective committees and show that the Minister of Militia was a member. The committee, however constituted, and whatever its personnel, was, from the time of its institution, a committee acting under the authority of the Imperial Government.
This country is innocent, this House must be innocent, to believe that the Solicitor General did not know who were the members of the Shell Committee, and did not even know that the Minister of Militia was a member of that committee. He concludes his argument, and this is what I deem to be the best portion of it, with these words:
If we have the right to review part of the moneys that are payable to the Imperial Government we have the right to review all the expenditures in which .we are interested. We are interested in the same degree in the money paid by the Imperial Government in the United States as in the- money paid in Canada. We have to pay some part of that, and we have to pay some part of the, money that has been

spent in Japan, and in Great Britain itself, and if there is a duty upon the Parliament of Canada to investigate the expenditure of Imperial moneys for the munitions of Canada, the same duty must apply to all the moneys in which we are interested expended by the Imperial authorities.
Are we interested in the money spent in Japan? If we are, we recognize that this Government, in the exercise if its plenary powers, has no jurisdiction over Japan. Everybody knows that. The Solicitor General stiys that we would have jurisdiction over the money spent in Japan if this Government had jurisdiction over the money that has been spent in this country and given to persons under- the control of this Government.
The Minister of Finance, speaking in Toronto, gave us a further inkling into what was being done in connection with financing the contracts entered into iby the Shell Committee. Here is the language he used when speaking to the Toronto Board ,of Trade:
Now in addition to that the Finance Department has advanced to the Imperial Treasury, in order to make payment for commitments of the Shell Committee in Canada, no less a sum than 63 million dollars.
That 63 million dollars has been repaid to Canada from time to time by the Imperial Treasury. But this is the point to which I want to call your attention. How has it been paid?
I had a statement from my deputy this morning in which he states that it has been paid by gold to the extent of many millions of dollars. In fact to the extent of 15 million dollars actually shipped in to the Finance Department. That is one reason why Canada has more gold to-day than she had when the war broke out, in liquidation for advances made to the Imperial Treasury for the purpose of financing the Shell Committee.
In addition to that, payment has been made by exchange operations, on which there would be a heavy discount, running from 3 to 5 per cent, amounting to over 20 million . dollars.
And he proceeds with his very a-ble speech. However, he tells us, and this I want to lay down as one of the premises of my argument, that the money of Canada, over which this Government have absolute control, was expended in payment of contracts entered into by the Shell Committee. We have at least jurisdiction over the money that this Government expends; hon. gentlemen opposite will admit that. Whether that money is paid by way of advances, or by way of loans, or otherwise, the moment the money of Canada has been paid this Parliament has jurisdiction over the expenditure.
I think hon. gentlemen who are just will admit that. My hon. friend the member for

St. John (Mr. Pugsley), on the 13th day of April, 1915, asked a question of the Minister of Militia in regard to the following article which appeared in the Ottawa Free Press of the previous day:
Revelations of war purchases on boots, bandages, binoculars and bad horses apparently have crossed the Atlantic.
It looks as if the British Government had begun to sit up and take notice. Soon after the opening of the war the British Government entrusted the Canadian Government with the purchasing of some war supplies in Canada for the use of the British and allied forces. The British Government was to pay the bills.
It is understood that within the last few days the War Office or the British Government has cancelled the buying commissions which it gave to the Canadian Government.
This does not mean an end to the purchase of supplies in Canada by the British Government, as War Office buyers are on their way to Canada and the United States, and hereafter the British Government will deal direct with producers and manufacturers on this continent without the intervention of Ottawa.
My hon. friend from St. John based a question on that article, the purpose of which I take to be that up to date the Canadian Government alone had full control of these purchases, that they had been purchasing for the Imperial Government, if you will, but that it was the intention of the Imperial Government to deal directly with manufacturers in Canada without the intervention of Ottawa. My hon. friend from St. John proceeded to say:
I ask the Minister of Militia if the Government has received notice from the British War Office that they are sending their agents to the United States and Canada for the purpose of making purchases direct from the manufacturers, and are not to continue making them through my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and others who have been appointed by him?
Major General Hughes:	The hon. gentleman
asks me a question concerning the Department of Militia, and I am in the happy position of being able to answer him. There is not a word of truth in that article, so far as the Department of Militia is concerned. So far as the Government is concerned the Prime Minister is the proper gentleman to ask.
Sir Robert Borden:	The statements in the
article are absolutely without foundation, so far as I am aware. On the contrary, I know that within the past four or five days the British Government have asked the Canadian Government to act in respect of the procuring of a large amount of supplies in Canada for the War Office.
So that it would appear that up to this date the British Government had absolutely no agents in this country for the purchase of war supplies. I take it that the British Government had asked the 'Canadian Government to act in the matter, and that the Canadian Government would appoint

their agents to purchase any supplies that might be required by the War Office and could be got in Canada. In corroboration of my statement that the British Government had no agents in this country at that time, I refer to a question asked in the British House of Commons on the 15th of March, just exactly one month before the hon. member for St. John asked his question in this House. Mr. MacVeagh, a member of the British House, asked the Undersecretary of State for War:
Whether the contracts being placed in Canada and the United States, are being placed by special agents, and if so, what is their commercial experience; whether the remuneration is by salary or commission, and if so. how much; and whether the co-operation of the Canadian Government has been invited?
Mr. Baker, who was then Financial Secretary to the War Office, replied:
Messrs. J. P. Morgan & Company, of New York, who are in close touch with all the American markets, have been appointed commercial agents to the Government for the purpose of placing orders in the United States. Their remuneration is by commission, but it is not considered to be in the public interest to give the details of the contract.
The British Government then, had agents in the United States, and their agents were Messrs. J. P. Morgan and Company. But as regards Canada Mr. Baker proceeded to say:
No special agents have been appointed for purchasing in Canada. Close touch has been maintained with the Canadian Government in regard to orders placed in that country.
According to the War Office, then, the Canadian Government had absolute control of all purchases and over all contracts entered into in this country. Now at this time the Shell Committee had been formed by the Minister of Militia, and in the report which was laid on the table by the Prime Minister on the 15th of April last, General Bertram speaks of the Shell Committee as follows:
In addition to the foregoing, the 1 Minister of Militia, through his committee-
Through " his " committee, mark you, General Bertram was supposed to be the chairman of the committee that was supposed to be the go-between with the manufacturers of Canada and the Imperial Government, and he says that the committee was not the committee of the Imperial Government, but the committe of the Minister of Militia of Canada. The committee was formed, then, by the Minister of Militia, who was at that time and is now a member of this Government. The Shell Committee
was absolutely under his control and under the control of the Canadian Government, and reported to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Militia. The fact is, however, that the only report which has been laid upon the table as coming from the Shell Committee was made directly to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister of Canada. General Bertram, in another part of his report, uses this language:
We informed the various officials at the War Office that it was the intention of the Minister of Militia and his committee-
Again it is "his" committee. Throughout his whole report Colonel Bertram spoke of the Shell Committee as the committee of the Minister of Militia, and as the commitee of the Canadian Government. The Right Hon. Mr. Baker, the Financial Secretary of the War Office, made in the British House <5f Commons the statement that the War Office had no agents in Canada, that the Canadian Government was making the purchases. It appears from this debate, and from what papers we have in our possession, that the Canadian Government controlled every contract that was entered into with the manufacturers, that they had absolute control over the Shell Committee, over the appointment of inspectors, and over every other detail of the committee's work. The Solicitor General, speaking of the Shell Committee, said:
They conducted their business directly with the Imperial authorities. Communications passed from the Shell Committee to the Imperial Government and from the Imperial Government to the Shell Committee. Had they been in a position where we had authority over them, had they been constituted as a committee under a department of this Government-
And you must mark General Bertram's statement that the committee was a committee of the Minister of Militia.
-they would have been answerable to this Government; we would have had authority over them and we would have been reaponsible.
In view of these statements; in view of the statement of General Bertram, the chairman of the Shell Committee, that the committee was a committee under the Department of Militia; in view of the statement of the Solicitor General that the Shell Committee had direct communication with the Imperial Government when it is in proof and in evidence that this communication was directly with the Minister of Militia and the Prime Minister of this country, and in view of the fact that the Solicitor General said that if the Shell Committee had been constituted as a committee under a department of this Government, they would have

been answerable to this Government,-when we have the Minister of Militia telling us yesterday that he was the father of the committee, and when we have the evidence that it was a committee under the Department of Militia, I ask this Government and the Solicitor General, what further excuse will the Government give to the people of Canada for refusing the investigation which has been asked by the Opposition, and which is being asked by the people of this country?
I feel that I have spoken at greater length than I had intended, and as I am about to resume my seat I want to say that I believe it to be the first duty of this Government and of the people of this country to see this war brought to a successful issue; but at the same time I want to remind the Minister of Finance, before he puts on any more taxes, that his raising of duties last year has simply had the effect of adding to the burdens of the consumer and of protecting a class already protected in this country, namely, the manufacturers. I would like to recall to him the language used by the Right Hon. Mr. Asquith in the British House of Commons:
If there is one thing that is axiomatic in fiscal theory and practice, it is this, that you cannot combine in one and the same imposition a revenue and a protective duty.
So far the increase in the duty has failed to give us the revenue we require; so far the increase in the duty has borne heavily upon the consumer, and yet we are obliged, in order to meet the ordinary expenditure, to go out and borrow. I have said, and I repeat that we have in this country untold wealth, agricultural, mineral, and industrial. I want to say to the Government: You should see to it that you do not rely upon your customs duties as your source of revenue. Your greatest source of revenue is in the wealth produced by your agriculture; it is your basic wealth, protect it. You are asking the farmers to produce more. They are the only unprotected class in this country, and yet you are taxing the essentials which they require, and without which they cannot clear the additional land necessary for increased production; they cannot build the additional buildings necessary to hold the greater volume of crops; they cannot till the soil and reap the harvest. You are increasing those burdens already on their shoulders by increasing your duties without thereby increasing your rev-9 p.m. enue. Now is the time for the Government to lay down a sys-
tem for securing immediately after this war the best possible class of immigrants. Now is the time for them to lay down a system by which they will perfect the means of transportation by rail and by water- Now is the time for them to develop the mineral resources of this country, to save the forests, to lessen industrial disputes by giving due regard to the grievances of the labouring classes. In the different departments of the public service, now is the time for the Government to abolish the patronage system, and to call to their service the best class of officials obtainable, and to pay them a just wage. I have always had unbounded confidence in the future of my country. I believe that our people have awakened to the great possibilities of Canada, and whilst we are assuming tremendous financial obligations, I believe that by a judicious and economic expenditure and administration, in spite of the awful strain upon this country caused by the depression through which we have passed and by the war, we shall again be able to travel upon that road upon which we had made such headway before 1911, in building up this country and bringing it on towards nationhood.

Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me, I would like to add my congratulations to those which have already been offered to you on your elevation to the high and honourable position which you occupy with so much grace and dignity. I would like also to offer my congratulations to the mover and to the seconder of the Address on the able and eloquent manner in which they discharged their duties.
Speeches in Parliament on the Address and on the Budget may be taken as giving a fair index of the popular mind on questions of public interest. At this particular time, when the liberties of mankind are in the balance, and when the very foundations of civilization are being threatened, the utterances of public men are of more than ordinary interest. Many of the speeches which have been delivered in this debate have been free from partisanship. That does not, in my estimation, indicate by any means that the members who delivered those speeches are less party men than they formerly were, but if they have ha<J grievances, they have felt that at the present time and under existing circumstances they had better hide those grievances or grieve inwardly, so to speak, and wait for another

opportunity of attacking the Government on matters in regard to which, in their opinion, the Government should be attacked. But all the speeches which have been delivered in this House have not been free from partisanship. So far as the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) is concerned, I have no fault to find; in fact, I most cordially agree with many of his utterances.
I do not agree with his views on some matters, and 1 will briefly refer to a few of the points on which I am at variance with him.
In his remarks on the purchase of the submarines, he stated that his complaint was that the price paid was too high for obsolete vessels. He did not question the' necessity for these vessels and therefore did not question their usefulness. We have the statement made by a responsible minister of the Crown from British Columbia, that these vessels were of the greatest use in protecting the coast cities of Victoria and Vancouver. It does seem to me that when we consider the situation of Victoria and Vancouver at the outbreak of the war, we must see that the knowledge on the part of the German Government-and I think we may assume that Germany had that knowledge-that these submarines had been purchased, would have a very strong effect in preventing Germany from sending any of her cruisers so far away from their base of supplies. Fot my part, vl am willing to leave the matter of the submarines- to the consideration and judgment of the people of this country. I do not think the Government will be blamed; on the contrary I think the greatest credit will be given to those who effected the purchase of these submarines at that time.	.
The hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) said that a few years ago hon. members on this side of the House declared that we "should not have truck or trade with the Yankees." That statement has often been made in a general way-, but it has not been attributed to any individual. That was not the position taken by the Conservative party in 1911. We have never taken a position that we did not want to "truck or trade with the Yankees," but we did take the position-and which was diametrically opposed to the position taken by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his friends-that we were not prepared to allow this country to become a mere adjunct to the United States, and we were not prepared to hand over Canada to the United States. We were prepared then, and we are prepared to-day, to trade
with the people of the United States or any other people on a fair basis, but we are not prepared to give away this country, as hon. gentlemen opposite have been disposed to do on more than one occasion.
As to my hon. friend's criticism of the expenditure of money on post offices in small towns, I would remind him that previous to the	advent to power of
the party which he supports in 1896, there was a generally understood, though unwritten, law that these buildings should not be constructed in towns of less population than about five thousand, and previous 'to the coming into power of the Laurier Government there were very few deviations from that general Tule. If that rule was departed from, and if buildings were put up in small places at enormous expense to the country, that policy was introduced by the party which my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) supports.
The hon. gentleman made a statement with regard to the farmer, which, if I heard it correctly, I heartily endorse. He said that the farmer .should not be the only unprotected man in this country; that if the manufacturers were protected the farmers ought to be protected also.- If I am not giving correctly the substance of his words I hope he will correct me. Understanding the statement in that way, I heartily agree with it. But what was the position the hon. gentleman and Ihis friends took in 1911 with regard to the farmer when they proposed to this country their policy of reciprocity with the United States? They proposed by that policy to throw open the doors of Canada to every country of agricultural production on the face of the globe. That is the proposition they offered then and that is the policy that the country rejected. What would be the position of our farmers in Canada to-day had that policy been carried out? With the products of t'he various countries practically excluded from the markets of Europe, those markets being made very dangerous of access by the war, we may be quite certain that if there was a low price for any farm product in any part of the world, that low price would be given to the farmers- of Canada, for if our prices here at any time fell to a figure that would attract the producers of other countries, our farmers would have no protection, but the agricultural products of these other countries would be thrown into our market to the injury of our farming population.
Now, a word as to the hon. gentleman's

observations concerning the transactions of the Shell Committee, and his observations on this subject were almost in the same words as those used by other hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House. I wish, first, to make one or two quotations. At the time of the South African war, the good offices of the Laurier Government then in power, were given to Britain in the purchasing of supplies in Canada for the use of the British Government. In 1902 a resolution was moved in this House asking for an investigation in regard to these transactions. The investigation was refused on the ground that the war was in progress. Next year, 1903, the same request came up, and I will quote briefly to show the grounds on which that request for an investigation was then refused. The Minister of Finance of that time, Hon. W. S. Fielding, used these words:
If we loaned the good offices of any of the officials of Canada, I cannot admit that we thereby are liable to account to this House for any expenditure of Imperial money which may happen to have been made in that connection.
And here is a brief extract from the speech made by the Prime Minister of that time, now the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier):
We have had no complaint from the British Government and I therefore see no reason why this House should inquire into the expenditure of money which does not concern it.
That was the position taken by two of the most prominent members of the Liberal Government, and that position was endorsed by every member on the Liberal side of the House at that time. I cannot see that the position to-day is any different from what it was then. 'I might use the -very words used by the present leader of the Opposition and say: We have no complaint from the British Government in regard to the whole business. And if fair consideration be given to the facts stated here yesterday by the hon. Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes)
I think it will be seen that there is no cause for hon. gentlemen opposite to make the complaint that they do. tn the course of the speech of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) I asked a question of that gentleman. He was discussing the giving of a shell contract to some firm in St. Catharines. I asked him a very proper question, simply when the order was given to this company. 1 got no direct answer to that, and I repeat-

ed my question. Then the hon. member for Carleton appealed to the Chair and refused to give me an answer. Of course it is the privilege of any member to answer or not to answer a question that is put to him. The reason the hon. member for Car-leton did not answer the question was because, if he had answered it, it would have done away with the argument he was trying to advance, in so far as that one firm was concerned, because, as a matter of fact, that firm was not given an order for shells at that time, but an order for cartridge cases, and so did not come within the line of argument the gentleman was pursuing.
My hon. friend from Carleton has told us that he does not allow the Ottawa Free Press to speak for him. The Free Press is to be congratulated in that it does not have to speak for the hon. member for Carleton, or to endorse what he says. The hon. member left out one thing in his speech this year. Last session he rang the changes on two men whom he called Bill and Dan. in future, I expect, it will be Sir William ai d Sir Dame' with the hon. member for Carleton. Why? Because during the past summer Sir William and Sir Daniel gave the hon. member for Carleton a free ride across this continent, and he came back so extremely mellowed that it is now Sir William and Sir Daniel, and he is ready to swallow one-half or two-thirds of what he said about them in this House last session. The Government has no right to complain of criticism; and although at this time, with the war in progress, they might expect that some of the harsher criticism should be postponed, yet they naturally do expect to get an occasional shot from the other side. But while they may be willing to submit to a little political sniping from some hon. gentlemen opposite, I do think, and I am sure the country will agree with me in this, that they have a right to expect that hon. gentlemen opposite should not use poison gas in their attacks. As far as the hon. member for Carleton is concerned, when his hand grenades or rather his mouth grenades, his shrapnel and high explosives and his sniping failed to make a hit, he undertook to make use of the poisonous gas of misrepresentation; and, a very short time after he had started that gas in the direction of the Government, the wind changed and it was blown back in his own face, and he has gone away now, pretty sick. So far as his very wild statements concerning shell contracts, etc., are concerned, the speech of the Minister

of Militia is the fullest and most complete answer. In so far as his equally wild and reckless statements concerning the purchase of hay are concerned, I should think that the hon. member for Oarleton, N.B., would never mention hay again. He was very much concerned about the farmers of his county. Contracts for hay had been let and the farmers had been paid $11, $12.50, $13 a ton for the hay; and he said they were being bled in the interests of favourites of the Government. He shed very copious tears for the farmers in his county. He told us that not only were they prohibited from exporting by an embargo on the export of hay but, worse than that, hay was being brought by the schooner load from the Annapolis valley of Nova Scotia in competition with the product of the farmers in his part of the country. He said:
The whole intention is to show the farmers of New Brunswick that they can get the 15,000 tons of hay without them, and make them accept the price they are willing to pay.
In other words, we see the reason for the action of the hon. member for Carleton when he was buying hay to ship over to England at the time of the Boer war, because he admitted that he brought in several carloads from Quebec for the express purpose, unquestionably, as he puts it here himself, of showing the farmers in his part of the country that it was possible for him to get the hay elsewhere, and thus forcing them to accept the seven or eight dollars a ton he was kind enough to give them-Not only that, but he himself made a binding contract with the sub-contractors, holding them down in such a way that they dare not buy hay from the poor farmers at a higher price than he wanted to, pay, or otherwise the punishment clause in the contract would be invoked, and they would be subject to a penalty. Never since I have had the honour of a seat in this House have I seen any person make such reckless statements as the hon. member for CaHeton made, statements which, if applied to his own conduct a few years ago, would meet the condemnation from his own mouth which he was trying to place on members on this side of the House. Not alone in regard to hay did the hon. member speak; he also had something to say about horses. He said:	In
regard to fifty horses which were offered, by Mr. Cox:
When Sir Adam Beck was put In charge, for some accountable reason, I do not know why, he refused this gift; he sent around other' veterinary inspectors, and they refused to accept every one of these fifty horses. Then the man who had charge of these horses-I think that perhaps Mr. Cox may have had a little finger in the pie as well-decided to test the sincerity of those who were acting for the Government in this matter. Mr. Cox said: We will see how serious these men are in their rejection of these horses.
And so on. I have in my hand the .Toronto Daily Star, of Wednesday, January 26, and, since the hon. member for Carleton introduced the name of Mr. Cox in this matter, I want to quote w'hat Mr. Cox himself says in regard to this transaction, and then leave it to the judgment of the House how far they can rely upon statements made by the hon. member for Carleton. The Toronto Daily Star is a Liberal paper. The article to which I refer is headed:
H. C. Cox Drops Thousands on Horses. Came back on his hands because Mounted Units went as Infantry.
This is what Mr. Cox has to say in regard to this matter:
If there is any insinuation that the horses were unfit, or that there was anything irregular about the transaction in regard to these horses, in all fairness to the Government and myself it ought to be cleared up, though ordinarily I do not care to add anything in debates of this kind, where politics are to some extent involved. I am honourary colonel of the 9th Mississauga Horse, of which H. D. Lockart Gordon, now at the front, is the colonel. He was very anxious to have the regiment go to the front as a mounted unit, and so I bought flfty horses for the boys to take out to camp at Long Branch for training purposes, and the city bought them fifty more. The bodyguard also were furnished with fifty horses hy the city and flfty by Mr. Aemilius Jarvis, the honorary colonel of that regiment. These horses were brought in with the regiment when they went into winter quarters at Exhibition Camp but when these troops finally were ready to leave for the front the Government decided not to send them as mounted troops, but as dismounted cavalry, or infantry, until such time as conditions at the front warranted the use of horsemen as such. Consequently I was left with fifty horses on my hands, horses which had cost on the average of $200 each. I sold some of them at Grand's stable, and some-I do not know how many; it may have been twelve,, as stated-were sold to the Government Commission's Purchasing agent for remounts, or for whatever purpose they were required. I dropped several thousand dollars over the matter from first to last, but I only mention it now to clear up any misapprehension that may he raised by the discussion in the House of Commons yesterday.
Mr. Cox, who is a well known Liberal, whose sympathies are naturally with the party on the other side of the House, makes the statement that he does not wish any insinuation to be made that the horses



were unfit, or that there was anything irregular in the transaction; and he makes it as a matter of fair play, not only to himself, but to tije Government as well. Now, Sir, that is certainly a very different attitude from that taken by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., and conveys a very different impression. Why is it that the hon. member for Carleton took the course he did? Why is it that he plainly misrepresented the facts in regard to the horses, in regard to the shells, and in regard to the hay? What is it for, if it is not for this: That he believes that by circulating such reckless statements in the press they will have some political effect.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell)* stated this afternoon that he had had certain talks with the hon. member for Carleton, who asserted that the Minister of Agriculture had requested him for God's sake not to bring up the matter of the purchase of the hay. That does not seem reasonable on the face of it. It is apparent, however, that there were some confidential talks between the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Carleton. The only explanation I can think of is to be found in the statement of the minister himself, that he had been sick for some time. He was not exactly himself, and was thrown off his guard a little; for surely the Minister of Agriculture has been long enough in this House, and has had sufficient opportunity of judging the calibre of the hon. member for Carleton to know that a man, who would have no regard for his country at a time like this, would not be persuaded even for God's sake not to bring up a matter if there was any political capital to be made out of it.
In regard to the matter of shells and the profits on shells, however, I observe that there was one -company which the hon. member for Carleton handled very lightly indeed. That was the company which bears the name of the Canada Foundry and Forgings Company, a company in which the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is very deeply -interested. The hon. member for Carleton was not so anxious to have an inquiry regarding that company, not -so anxious to know how it was that the -stock of that -company rose within ten days from 30 to 260, unquestionably making some person very wealthy. He passed very lightly over that and went on, to make reckless statements regarding other companies.

In regard to the matter of exorbitant profits on war materials, I wish to state, Mr. Speaker, that I endorse the words of the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin); and I will endorse the words of any hon. gentleman in this House who takes the position that at this time of stress and strain no man, or firm, should make large profits out of munitions or anything else that is being furnished for the'prosecution of the war. The people of the Dominion of Canada have responded nobly to appeals in support of the Red Cross, the Patriotic Fund, the Belgian Relief and other funds, and I say that no greater shame could attach to any man in Canada after this war is over than to be pointed out as one who had made hundreds of thousands of dollars out of exorbitant profits on anything furnished for the prosecution of the war. That is the position I take; that is the position which I understand the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) took in his sp'eeeh, which statement on his part I thoroughly endorse.
At present there are millions of poor Belgians who have been driven out of their own country, refugees who are being taken care of in foreign lands; there are others in that country huddling around the ruins of their shattered villages, waiting for their turn to get a meal that will keep them alive from one day to the next; women in tattered garments, with little children hanging to their skirts, standing in the snow waiting for the free meals; and I repeat that nothing could be more shameful than for any man in the Dominion of Canada to go through this war making excessive profits while those conditions obtain.
I believe that, since this great task was thrown upon its shoulders, the present Government has done everything in its power to try to prevent profiteering, if I may use that Word. The burdens thrown upon this Government have been enormous. That fact has been recognized by many hon. gentlemen on the opposite side who have spoken. Mistakes have unquestionably been made, but I believe that if you put the question to the people in the Dominion of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, ninety-nine per cent, would say that, in its conduct of this war, the Borden Government has been actuated by the desire to do the best that Canada could possibly do, and by a desire to prevent any grafting or exorbitant profits. They have given ample evidence of that in the past, day after day, and month after month; and

the attacks which have been made by one or two hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House, especially by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley)' and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), are not to the credit of these gentlemen. It has been shown that these attacks Avere made recklessly, and without that due regard for the truth which ought to characterize the remarks of these hon. gentlemen, and of every other hon. gentleman in this House. I am quite confident that, when the proper time arrives, the people of this country will mete out to these hon. gentlemen the condemnation which they richly deserve.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) informed us that he had been asked to address a recruiting meeting in St. James Methodist church, Montreal. I am sure that the hon. member for Rouville has advertised that so thoroughly himself throughout the country that he will not object to a reference to it by myself. He should be very grateful to the Methodist church in general, and to St. James Methodist church in Montreal in particular for giving him the splendid opportunity of letting the "world know his breadth of vision, how broad and loyal he is and how fearless. He told us that he addressed that meeting and that he was enabled to say that all churches should be recruiting tents. A so-called religious paper took him to task for making such a statement as that. I commend the hon. member for Rouville for his splendid courage, for we must suppose that he exhibited courage. He spoke himself as though he had, anyway. But I want to tell the hon. member for Rouville that in the province of Ontario we wonder at him mentioning the thing at all, because in Ontario every Protestant church since this war started has been thrown open as a recruiting tent, and every. Protestant minister in Ontario-I do not speak for the other provinces, but I suppose it is the same- has been in the forefront of all movements for advancing the cause of Great Britain in connection with this war, as we would wish to see it, whether in connection with recruiting, getting money for patriotic funds, or for relief funds, or in connection with other such movements, and, to their honour be it said, that they have taken a very active part in this respect. The hon. member for Rouville, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain), and the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) quoted some very noble utterances of certain of -the higher clergy of their church. I have 234
no fault to find with that; it is quite proper that they should take pride in their church and in what their church is saying, but if we were -to quote the splendid and noble words which have fallen from the lips of Anglicans, Methodists, Presbyterians and members of other denominations in this country, I am afraid we would spend several days and take up needlessly a great many pages of Hansard. It is true that religious denominations will be judged in this war to a certain extent by what the adherents of these denominations have done in the way of recruiting; and it is true that a great deal of consideration will be given to the remarks of. bishops, archbishops, and clergymen in general at the heads of these churches. That is as it should be. We expect, not only the clergy of the Protestant denominations, but we expect the priests of the Roman Catholic faith, and we expect the Pope himself, the head of that great body, to be on our side in this war. Why it is necessary to call particular attention to their utterances I fail to see inasmuch as certainly no person has made any charge to the contrary. No person has charged them with lack of loyalty or of zeal in this House -or, as far as I have heard, in the country.
But after all, the men who are most deserving of our praise and admiration are not really the bishops and clergy who have expressed noble sentiments in Canada, but they are the hundreds of Roman Catholic priests and Protestant clergymen who today are sharing the trials and dangers of the men in the trenches in Flanders. They are the men to whom I take off my hat every time, and I ask not what denomination they belong to, but I pay them the highest tribute that it is possible to pay those men for their heroic self-sacrifice.
The Tight hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) referred briefly to conscription. He quoted from a paper published on the other side of the line to show that some of those Americans, who had come into the Northwest in hundreds of thousands, had, since this war started,, gone back to the United States, and the right hon. -gentleman deplored that. The only thing I have to say in regard to that is. " good riddance." If they left this country-beoause they w'er-e afraid that they would have to fight for the country in which they lived and went back to the United States, I say: good riddance, let them go and stay away. This country has not lost

very much if'they go there and stay there. The leader of the Opposition uttered this sentence which caught my eye: The only .complete victory which has been won during this war has been won by the British navy. I think that statement is literally and absolutely correct. This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that the British navy has been a guarantee of the liberties of the people of Europe. It is not the first time that the British navy has prevented some powerful European monarch from realizing his ambitious ends. Phillip of Spain, Louis XIV of France, and Napoleon, all were checked in their ambitions by the navy of Britain, and, as in the days gone by, the task is forced upon Britain to-day of preventing a tyrant from grinding democracy beneath the iron heel of militarism.
The fate of the democracies of the world rests upon the British sea power. It is not England alone whose existence is at stake. I make that statement because once in a while we hear some person say that this is " England's war." This is not England's war any more than it is Canada's war. It is not only the freedom and rights of the people of the British Islands, or of the British Empire, that is at stake, but it is the freedom and rights of the democracies of the world. When the curtain falls on the last act of this great war, it will disclose the faces,-the joyful faces-of those who are sure of their freedom; or it will disclose the solemn and sad faces of people who have been bereft of everything they hold most dear.
This is not merely a fight of England against Germany ; it is a fight for supremacy between two irreconcilable principles-democracy on the one hand, as represented by England and France, and autocracy, or militarism, on the other hand, as represented by Germany and her allies. It is a struggle for freedom against slavery, and against a slavery worse than that which bound the negro to his master. This is a struggle to maintain democratic rights and true Christian principles against a country which has accepted the teachings of Treitsche and Bernhardi as being more infallible than the teachings of Christ, and which deifies and worships naval and military power as the most sublime of all religions. If it had not been for the British navy, France would, long ere this, have been crushed, Russia's power would have been broken, and the British Empire would have been shattered. The British fleet has swept the seas clear of German merchant

vessels and has driven the German war vessels behind their line of forts for safety. It has adequately protected ten billion dollars of Empire trade and $160,000,000,000 of Empire wealth; it has kept free from invasion, over 14,000,000- square miles of British territory and it has kept free of fire and sword the homes of over 400,000,000 people within the British Empire.
The British navy has preserved Canadian homes from destruction, Canadian women from outrage, and Canadian children from mutilation. Canadian commerce has been safeguarded, and Canadian liberty guaranteed by the British navy, which has been assisted by Australia, by New Zealand, by Newfoundland, and by all the overseas dominions except Canada. The fault or blame for the fact that Canada has not also assisted that navy lies not with men on this side of the House, but with hon. gentlemen opposite, and their servile and subservient Senate across the way. It has been said that Canada's first line of defence is in Flanders, but Sir, Canada's last line of defence, Canada's bulwark, Canada's guarantee, is that mighty, silent, eveT-watchful fleet in the North Sea, which hon. gentlemen opposite refused us the Tight to strengthen and make more effective. Those are the facts, and no ofie in this House can refute them. But these facts do not appeal to all men in this country. This protection of Canada's rights and of Canadian women and children does not appeal to the callous heart of Bourassa and Lavergne. It stirs their blackened blood to no quicker beat. Loyalty is not an abstract principle like truth, or honesty or charity; it depends upon the ideal, the motives by which one is actuated. The British idea of loyalty, for instance, forced King John to sign Magna Charta, took the head off Charles I, and replaced, James II with William and Mary. The people of the United' States in 1776 considered loyalty a crime and disloyalty the greatest of virtues. So it seems that loyalty is a virtue or a vice according to circumstance, and that a man may be a rebel or a patriot according as he backs a winning or a losing cause. But, by whatever standard you judge Bourassa.and Lavergne there is nothing that can be said in their defence. The right hon. leader of the Opposition had occasion to refer to them in his speech the other day. While he did not mention them by name, I think he unquestionably was alluding to these men. He said:
There has been a minority which has always protested against our attitude, and that minority

is the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec, who took the position from the start that it was a crime for the Canadian people to participate in this war. Not only did they use that strong language, but again and again in the Nationalist press they have asserted, and still assert, that we have taken our present position simply because we are subject to the imperious dictation of the British authorities.
Further on he says, and I wish to place his words on Hansard:
There may be and often is servility to a master; there may be and there is servility to passion and prejudice. And if to-day there is servility anywhere it is not with those who have taken the attitude which we have maintained, and will maintain in this House, but it is with those who, blinded by passion and prejudice, would deny us the liberty of being humane and generous, would deny us the liberty of following the instincts and promptings of our minds, and our hearts, and our consciences; would deny us the liberty, when wo see France threatened with dismantlement, when we see Belgium actually under the foot of the conqueror, of helping in the defence of France and of Belgium. It is not because they hate France, it is not because they hate Belgium, but because we cannot in this way help France or help Belgium without at the same time helping England. Sir, the case of France and the case of Belgium is the case of England. The case of England is the case of Belgium and France. Away with such sophistry. It is nothing but an attempt to conceal the hatred of empty minds. But, that is not all. These men also tell us that we may be fighting for an idea, as they say, and we may be fighting for the fate of the Empire, as they say, but that Canada has no direct or material interest in this war. And, every day we read in their press that if Germany were to triumph it would be of no material injury to Canada, that Canada would remain just in the position that Canada is in to-day.
Coming from a man who for fifteen years was prime minister of this country, a man from the province of Quebec, and who for practically his whole life has been the leader of a great party in this country, those words of his should give serious thought to every one of us in this House. He has made charges which are stronger than any that have ever been made against any party or sect in this country. A few years ago, I ventured to say from my place in this House that I believed there was ample evidence from the utterances of certain so-called leaders of the province of Quebec, to believe that there was in that province an antiBritish or anti-imperial sentiment, and I wa3 taken very severely to task for that statement. I did not charge them, nor do I charge now, nor have I ever charged, the mass of the people of Quebec with being disloyal. I made that as clear as words could make it, but I did charge that there were certain men who had assumed the positions of leaders in that province who
had been guilty of disloyal utterances and of taking a course which was inimical not only to the best interests of the people of the province of Quebec, but to the best interests of the country as a whole. Within a few months after I made that statement a by-election took place in the province of Quebec and the Government candidate was defeated. When the House met again a bitter' discussion took place between members on both sides of the House from the province of Quebec, and if I had wanted any corroboration of the charges I had made in the previous session, I got that corroboration from gentlemen on both sides of the House. The right hon. leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, who was then in the House, hurled charges against men on the opposite side of the House, accusing them of using disloyal language throughout the province of Quebec. Gentlemen on this side of the House charged the supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite with using disloyal language, and quoted from their speeches in proof of it. When these hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House got through, one thing at least was clear; and that was that in the province of Quebec there was a certain number of men who .thought that the best way to win an election in that province was to pound England and everything British, that the worse the things they said about England and everything British the more likely they were to get votes. But nothing that has been said in former sessions compares in severity with the language used by the right hon. leader of the Opposition the other day in regard to what are called the Nationalists in the province of Quebec, and I commend the right hon. gentleman for speaking, out so openly in regard to these so-called leaders of a party. The right hon. gentleman stated-and he is a man whose words ought to receive more attention than mine, and that is why I quote them-that from day to day the Nationalist press in the province of Quebec is making use of language that is a disgrace to the press in general, and to the province of Quebec in particular, and, Sir, when a paper makes use of such disgraceful and disloyal language it should be suppressed. I take it that the duty of suppressing it falls upon the Postmaster General, although I may not be correct in that regard. I presume he has carefully looked over Le Devoir, which, I believe, is the most offending paper; and if what is

stated in regard to that paper is true, or if only a small portion of it is true, then it is the duty of the Postmaster General to suppress that paper. If it is right to deny the use of the mails of this country to certain publications from the other side of the line because they are pro-German, and I say it is right; then it cannot be right to allow the publication in our own country of language which should not be used here, particularly at this time. Before suppressing any paper the Postmaster General should consider the matter very carefully. We must be tolerant and very careful in taking action against any paper; but we are engaged in a struggle at the present time when every man is required, and if there is being published in the province of Quebec or elsewhere in this country, papers which tend to -prevent the recruiting of that accumulation of men on which the very life of this country and this Empire may depend, then even while we may run the risk of being regarded as intolerant, there is a time when tolerance becomes cowardice.
I have not very much to say in regard to Mr. Bourassa. I would not mention his name at all were it not for the fact that at one time he occupied a seat in this House as a follower of the right hon. gentleman who at present leads the Opposition.
How was he last time?

Well, I was not in as close touch with him as the hon. member was, and I could not say, but I think there is pretty good evidence that he will be shaking hands with hon. gentlemen opposite in the next election.

How do you like him
now when he is supporting your party?

I am not aware that he is supporting our party. On the contrary, it seems to me that his opposition has been very pronounced against our party. He has [DOT]done everything a man can possibly do *against the successful conduct of this war. How, the hon. gentleman can draw on his imagination to such an extent to say that this man is a supporter of the present Government, I cannot understand.
He will probably have a. seat in this House in the next Parliament.

It may be that'the gentleman to whom I refer will have a seat in this House in the next Parliament, but if that is the case, it will remain as an everlasting blot and disgrace on the constituency that gives him that seat in the next Parliament.
I'Mr. Edwards. ]
He will not be any worse than the ministers you have got on your side now.

Apparently supporters
of this gentleman to whom I refer are not confined to this side of the House. My hon. friend across the way seems quite warm in his regard for this man who has published treason from one end of the country to the other.
There is another man to whom I wish to refer, who bears the name of
10 p-m. Armand Lavergne, and I would not refer to him, were it not for the fact that he had a seat in this House behind the present leader of the Opposition of whom he was a supporter. All that I have to say in regard to that gentleman is this: he holds, I understand, the rank of colonel in the militia of Canada, and I want to say, speaking for myself alone, that I regard it as a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada that a man of the stamp of Armand Lavergne should be allowed to retain his rank in the militia of Canada. I regard it not only as a disgrace to Canada, but as a distinct insult to every man who wears the King's uniform to-day, and I ask, Mr. Speaker, neither the gentlemen on this side of the House who apparently support Mr. Bourassa and Mr. Lavergne, nor the gentlemen on the other side whether they agree with me in that statement or not; but I am confident that most of the people of this country agree with me, and I would be very sorry to think that most of .the people of the province of Quebec did not agree with me, because I have talked with many people from that province who, to their eternal credit be it said, resent the conduct and language of these two men just as strongly as I do. Mr. Armand Lavgrgne's uniform should be taken from him; he should not be allowed to disgrace it. No man should be allowed to wear the King's uniform who uses the language that he has used. He has stood up in the legislature of the province of Quebec and defied his King and country. That is a disgrace to this country; it should not be tolerated in this country, and I ask the Government why it is tolerated. Why is he allowed to wear his uniform?
Ask your minister.

The only reason that I have thus far heard is this:	Oh, if you
take the uniform away from him, it is just what he wants; he wants to make a martyr of himself. Again I will express my

opinion-I am not presuming to express an opinion for others-that that excuse is nothing more nor less than an excuse of political cowardice. If he wants to be made a martyr of, then he should be made a martyr of- At all events he should not he allowed to disgrace the uniform which he has disgraced while holding the rank of colonel.
Although only a humble member on the Government side of the House, I will make this suggestion to the Government, that they open up negotiations with Germany through the mediation of the United States or China or some other neutral nations for an exchange. Let them propose to give Bourassa and Lavergne in exchange for Dr. Beland, and let them throw in one or two of the senators over the way, notably Senator Choquette. They can make the proposition to Germany.
But I tell you, Sir, that if the proposition were made in all seriousness to Germany to give Lavergne and Bourassa, with Choquette thrown in, in exchange for Dr. Beland, Germany, bad as she is, vile as she is, would indignantly refuse; because if there is one thing that Germany detests more than another, it is treachery to the country in which a man lives.
I wish to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) in his speech in this debate. The hon. gentleman quoted some words of Edward Blake. They were not the words of Edward Blake in regard to the unrestricted reciprocity campaign of 1891, but they had reference to another matter. The words quoted were to the effect that a majority in dealing with a minority should give measure full, heaped up and running over-that is the measure to be given by the strong to the weak. And the hon. member for Rouville, commenting on these words says " May we not expect that there will arise another Blake to protect the Ontario minority? " I fully endorse those words of Edward Blake, but I want to tell the hon. member for Rouville that there is no necessity for an Edward Blake in Ontario for the purpose indicated by him. If there is any portion of the people of Ontario who need some person to champion their cause it is not the minority but the majority.
The hon. member for Rouville on several occasions has referred somewhat sneeringly, or slightingly-perhaps " slightingly " is better than " sneeringly," not so harsh at least-to the Orangemen of this country.
I want to say to the hon. member for Rouville that a gentleman who has occupied the position he has occupied in this country should be above such things. And I want to remind him of this fact-that there went in the first contingent from Valcartier more Orangemen than have been enlisted up to date in the province of Quebec, outside the city of Montreal.
Mr. LEMIEUX Does the hon. gentleman refer to anything in my speech in this debate, or what expression of mine concerning Orangemen is it to which he refers?

I did not quote the
words of the hon. gentleman.
Where did I speak in that way about the Orangemen? Where did I say anything about them at all?
On many occasions.
Let the hon. gentleman cite one.

Well, it was not a use of the word "Orangeman," but the other day, referring to events which took place in England on the 15th of July, when asked with regard to the date by a gentleman near him, the hon. gentleman turned, and with a queer smile, said: The Fifteenth of July, not the Twelfth of July.
Is that all?
That is all in that particular case, but there are other cases.

There arc none. Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of brder. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) has stated that I have on several occasions referred in a sneering way to the Orangemen. I declare to the House that I never made any reference to the Orangemen either from my place in this House or elsewhere in this country.	.
After that declaration on the part of the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) I think it is the duty of the hon. member for Frontenao (Mr. Edwards) to accept the explanation.

I cheerfully accept the hon. gentleman's explanation. I do not just know what reason he had for saying, "not the Twelfth of July" in the way he did. I have not at present under my hand words that he has used on former occasions, therefore I accept his statement.

You will never find

There is another remark of the right hon. leader of the Opposition to which I wish to refer, a remark to the effect that in the matter of participation in the wars of the Empire there was a distinct line of cleavage between himself and the present Prime Minister. I am very sorry that the right hon. leader of the Opposition reiterated that statement of former years; I am sorry that he still thinks it politically advisable to occupy an equivocal position as regards the future of this country and its participation in the destinies of the Empire. I cannot refrain from asking if "the goal of independence'' to which he has sometimes referred is still his great aspiration. What does he mean when he says that there is a great line of [DOT] cleavage between himself and the Prime Minister in regard to Canada's participation in the wars of the Empire? If his words have any meaning they presuppose that Great Britain, or the Empire, may be engaged in a life and death struggle about something of which Canada might not approve. The minor troubles of Great Britain would not affect Canada, as the right hon. gentleman knows. If our assistance was required it could only be in some trouble which might pull the Empire down, and whether we wished it or not, Canada would stand or fall by the result.
The right hon. gentleman made it clear that his policy is still the policy of semidetachment. There can be no other meaning to the words he has used. He would ask Parliament for its judgment in regard to our participation in any war in which the Empire might be engaged. What position would the right hon. gentleman be in if, in an emergency such as we have at present, he had behind him men like Bourassa and Lavergne who would, unquestionably,

if they did as they have 'been doing outside of this House, do all they could to delay and prevent any measure which he might bring down providing for participation. Suppose he had in this House such men as Myers, Farrer, Goldwin Smith, and others, who formed the Continental Union Association in 1892, the object of which was to bring about continental union, union between Canada and the United States. If he had such men as those who were in this country in 1892, an association, whose representatives in the province of Quebec as the firm of Mercier, Gouin, and Lemieux, carrying on that particular propaganda at that- time, writing across the line to moneyed men there, as the head of that firm did, for funds to assist him in carrying on that work, I think he would find himself in very serious difficulty in carrying out the ideas to which he has given expression. Therefore, I say, that in this matter of cleavage between the right hon. leader of the Government and the right hon. leader of the Opposition, I range myself alongside of the Premier who has given us to understand what his position is in regard to the Empire. I quote the words of the Prime Minister: :
So long as Canada remains in the Empire, Canada is at war when the Empire is at war. So long as the English flag floats above Canada, Canada is at war when that flag is attacked. The moment a shot is fired or a blow is struck at that flag, Canada is at war with the nation or country which fires that shot or strikes that blow.
That is the position taken by the Prime Minister of this country, and I have only to say that if there is a line of cleavage, which I very greatly regret, I want it to he understood on which side of the fine I stand. I believe our destiny is inseparably connected with Hire Mother Country, that if w*e are to work out what is in-the best interests of the Dominion of Canada this country must remain a part of the British Empire.
I believe I am expressing the sentiments of the people of this country when I say that they are prepared in the future to throw in their lot and stand or fall with the Mother Country. It means a lot more to be a Canadian to-day than it did a year and a, half ago, because of the position that Canada has taken in this war. All classes of the country have done their part well.

The students of the Royal Military College have brought very great credit to that institution and to all parts of the Dominion, inasmuch as they come from all parts of Canada. In 1914 the number of commissions^ taken in the Imperial army by the gentlemen cadets of the college was 50; in 1915 it was 22. In the Canadian Permanent
Forces 29 commissions were taken in 1914, and 39 in 1915. In the Canadian Overseas contingents, 24 commissions were taken in 1914 and 26 in 1915; or a total in 1914 of 103, and in 1915 of 87; or a grand total of 190. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is a record of which this country may well he proud, for I repeat that these students are drawn from every province in the Dominion. They have brought honour to every province, and their record at the front is certainly one of which we may well be proud.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker, in this debate. I am very sorry indeed if any words of mine in regard to the two men to whom I referred have hurt the feelings of any person in thi3 House. If it had not been for the fact that they occupied at one time seats in this House, that they are unquestionably prominent men in the country to-day, and men to whom the right hon. leader of the Opposition gives credit for having at least some influence, or who are trying to exert some influence in their province, I would not have referred to them at all. But I am impressed by the fact that this is a time when every nerve and sinew of the Empire is being strained, when we are up against a crisis which means either liberty or slavery; that this is a testing time for our country, not only for the men who have been recruited from the various parts of the country, but for the men who have been placed by the people in the positions which we occupy to-day. It is our business as public men to draw lessons and inferences from what we see happening around us, so that we can take our stand as public men and express our disapproval of language of an unpatriotic or disloyal character uttered in any part of this country, no matter by whom the words are uttered.
