I am one of those who believe that the manhood and womanhood of Canada have their hearts in this struggle, hoping and praying for the success of the allied arms. The other day the Postmaster General made a very nice and loyal speech in this House, but it struck me that it contained an apologetic note for the French race in this country. As the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has said, I believe the heart of Quebec is sound in this cause. I do not make that statement because of anything that has transpired in this war. As a student of Canadian history, I am bound to say that the French people of this country have time and again given every indication, every proof, if proof were needed, that their hearts are British, that they love the British flag, British traditions, British institutions, and the justice they get under the Union Jack. If proof were necessary, I should only have to turn back the pages of history to the American Revolution. In those days a standing offer was made to the French people along the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec to join the American revolutionists. The Freiich people spurned that offer. They remained true to the British flag, under which they have received more freedom than they could ever get under the flag of old France. If further proof were necessary, I could recall the other wars in which Canada has been engaged. I might refer to the war of 1812. Where, during that war, could you find throughout the length and breadth of Canada men more loyal to the cause of Britain than those French people who inhabited the banks of the St. Lawrence, Quebec. It is unneces-

sary for me to mention any names or regiments. I am not here championing the cause of Quebec, or apologizing for the French-Canadian people; for they need no apologists.
It is not necessary to prove that they are loyal either to this war or in any other. Their hearts are sound, as are the hearts of all English-speaking Canadians, and they are for the cause of the Allies and will stay with that cause. And people of all creeds, people of all denominations, and of' all classes in this country are giving and will give this Government every reason to believe that it will get all the support that is necessary in so far as Canada's participation in this world war is concerned.
I admit freely that this Government is doing well as regards recruiting in this country. They are doing well because the hearts of young and old Canadians are with the Government in sending overseas every available man and every man who will be necessary in order to win this war. Canadians, young and old, are with this Government in voting every cent and every dollar which is necessary for this purpose. While that is a fact, I deem it the duty of this Opposition to find fault with the Government if they think the Government has erred, or made mistakes in judgment, or anything else. I do not believe in abusing, or in criticising from personal motives, any hon. gentleman who occupies a portfolio in this Government, but I do say, in all sincerity, as a man who represents one of the largest * constituencies of working men in this country, that it is incumbent on hon. members of this House, whether they sit behind the Premier, or behind the leader of the Opposition, to criticise where criticism is necessary. We are engaged in a world struggle. We are engaged in a war that has caused more devastation in the few months it has been going on than any other war in history. We are engaged in a stiuggle the end of which no man knows, and in which every available man and every available dollar may haye to be used to bring it to a successful completion. That being the case, I say that we should conserve in all possible ways not only the health of the recruits we are sending overseas and those stationed in Canada, .but every possible dollar as well; and we should see that every dollar that is voted in this House finds its way into the proper channel. If members of the Opposition have reason to believe that the 
people's money is being diverted from the proper channels, if they believe that some of the $150,000,000 which this Parliament voted in the last two sessions is not being properly expended, if they believe they have some proof that the Government of this country is placing the expenditure of money in the hands of improper parties, if they believe that this money which was voted for the war is being given to contractors as rewards for political allegiance, then I say it is the duty of this Opposition to criticise and bring this state of affars to the attention of Parliament and the-country.

If the shell Committee spent that money honestly, * what fear has this Government of an investigation into the transactions of the Committee? If the Government does not wish the Shell Committee to be investigated, am I to believe that that committee spent the money dishonestly?

If the Government has no connection with the Shell Committee, if the Shell Committee is not responsible to this Government, not being its creature, if the committee was not bound to report to the Minister of Militia holding a portfolio in this Government, why then does the Government attempt to defend them? office. If they were spending properly the money entrusted to them to spend for England and for Canada, why should they have been removed at that time? If there
11 p.m. was no wrong doing, no harm is done; if there was wrong doing, it will be corrected and righted, and the people of this country will see that the public men on both sides of this House are willing to do right and not to shield the wrongdoer, be he Conservative or be he Liberal.
I have said that this Government has done well in the matter of getting our young Canadians to join the standard and to go overseas to fight the battles of the Empire.
If we take the words of the hon. Minister of Militia-and he should know-we have enlisted 250,000 men in this country to join the military forces of Great Britain; that 60,000 of those men are in or near the trenches in Flanders; that 60,000 are making preparations in England, and that the balance of 130,000 are in Canada training. A call has gone forth for an additional 250,000 men, making in all 500,000. I believe that our young Canadians will be recruited and that in less than a year that call for 500,000 men will be filled. Credit is due to the Government for having recruited these 250,000 men, and more credit will be given them if they succeed in recruiting the other 250,000 men. Let the Government be sure that they have the fullest co-operation of the Liberal party-at least of Liberals in the portion of the country from which I come, and that is the only part for which I desire to speak-in getting those recruits, as they have had ever since this war began. But while I am willing to make that statement, I am not willing to admit that the ministers of the Crown in this Government have done all that could be done in the matter of giving aid to the Mother Land and our Allies in this life and death struggle in which she is engaged. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) the other evening pointed out that all the other overseas dominions, Newfoundland, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa had contributed to the military forces of England not only as many men proportionately as Canada had done, but that they had also contributed thousands upon thousands of their young and best manhood to fill up the gaps in the British navy. My hon. friend the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) this evening commented on this fact, and by some curious device, by some .

sort of devilish sophistry, may I say, or by some sort of magnificent logic, came to the conclusion that the fact that this country was not represented by young Canadians in the navy of Great Britain, was to be placed at the door of the Liberal party. Let us follow that up.
This Government had a policy in naval affairs a few years ago. It was a policy of contribution-they proposed to contribute $35,000,000 to build three dreadnoughts for Great Britain. But has any member of the Government or any of its supporters ever said that the Canadian people were to contribute men as well as money to that navy? Such a policy was never enunciated. But the Liberal policy-we need not go into that in detail at this time-was to contribute ships for home defence and to participate in the wars of the Empire when necessary-These were not to be empty ships, but were to be commanded, manned and maintained by young Canadians. What has the Government done to contribute to the naval defence of Canada since this war began? Much was said a few years ago about the Niobe and the Rainbow; they were described as a " tinpot navy " by hon. gentlemen of Conservative persuasion. There was on the statute book of this country an Act known as a Naval Service Act, commonly known as the Laurier Navy Act. That Act, contrary to the views expressed by hon. gentleman opposite and contrary to the policy propounded by this Government, is still on the statute book and is still in full force and effect. Under that Act we had when the war broke out, and had had for some time previously, two war ships, one on the Pacific and one on the Atlantic. Those ships were allowed to go into disuse and disrepair. But immediately on the outbreak of the war the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) undertook to put these ships into commission, and we had it from him last session, that these ships, the Rainbow and the Niobe, were doing splendid work in coastal defence and in the transportation of soldiers and supplies. I would like to ask the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen), if he was right last year in so expressing his opinion of the Niobe and the Rainbow, why it is that the Niobe is dismantled and lying idle to-day in Halifax harbour? Why has not the minister sent out a call to the men of our seacoasts to fill up the gaps that have been caused in the British navy? I think the answer is that members of the Cabinet and their supporters told us a few 
years ago in this House that we could not get any such recruits in this country, and they do	not want	to	be	given	thelie. Because we can get such recruits in this	country	if	we call	for
them. We can certainly get a>-many in Nova Scotia as were contributed by the little colony of Newfoundland; we can get as many on the Pacific coast as were contributed by Cape Colony in South Africa. But it was not the policy of these hon. gentlemen opposite, and they do not want it to be thought that they knew nothing of the temper of the people in Canada who go down to the sea in ships, whether for fishing or for other purposes, on the Atlantic seaboard or on the Pacific coast. Much discredit, I am sorry to say, might be thrown upon the hon. gentleman who has charge of naval affairs, but I am not going into that just now. In our part of the country the state of affairs is rather too disgraceful to be dwelt upon in this House. But when the Minister of the Naval Service brings down his estimates we shall have something to say with regard to the vessels he sent out from certain ports in Nova Scotia to do patrol service along our coast-motor boats from ten to fifteen feet long sent down to the island of Newfoundland at a cost to this country of some $75 a day, to scare off German invaders who might come across in their armoured ships or submarines. For the present, we will let that matter rest.

Perhaps the hon. minister does not know all that is going on in his own department. He may be able, I will not say to mislead the House, but to make the House believe this, but he is certainly not going to make the people in the county and province from which I come believe it, for they have too much evidence to the contrary. I will submit that perhaps most of the plums in this crisis-if there are plums to give-under our system of Government -would naturally go to the friends of the party in power-
Not during war time.

-that is, when conditions are equal and the applicants on either side of politics are equally qualified to fill the positions-perhaps that will suit my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham). But when the Minister of Militia says that there are no

politics in the Department of Militia, I believe that every person in the province of Nova-Scotia who reads that statement, both his own political friends and those who are not his political friends, will blush for very shame. I do not say that some Grits did not find their way into commissions and into fairly good positions in the Militia; but whqt I do say that in the county from which I come the Militia Department is being used by the Conservative party as an addition to the party, as a caucus room, and that wherever recruiting stations are held in the county of Cape Breton there appears the agent of the Conservative candidate in that county. There was a time-
I am glad to say it has gone by now-when recruits were not accepted in that county until they had received the imprimatur of certain Conservative politicians in that county.
Give us some names.

Yes, I shall give names. The Minister of Public Works is strong on names, I shall give him names. Mr. Speaker, there is in our town a gentleman named Wm. McKinley. McKinley. There is in the town of Glace Bay what is known as the Marconi tower. Around that tower, since the outbreak of war there have been congregated 120 or 150 of Canada's militia. This man, Wm. McKinley he would hear more about it; with the result'that Mr. Wm. McKinley, whose only son is fighting and has been fighting in the trenches of Flanders ever 24
since the first Canadian expeditionary force went across, was deprived of that simple, small way of helping to earn a livelihood. Does the minister want some more names?
You have not answered me at all yet. My hon. friend perhaps misunderstood what he isaid himself. He siaid that applicants would not be accepted unless they were Conservatives.
If there is any way of misunderstanding, you would misunderstand.

The hon. member made a statement and said he would prove it.
Mr. CA'RROLL: Yes, I have made a statement,and I can prove it to the full.

If my hon. friend wishes names I will give them to him but I will not give them to him here.	,
I would like to get them now.

You will not. I may reply as the Minister of Militia replied to a question I asked yesterday. I asked for the regiment from Nova Scotia which was captained and officered wholly by Liberals. He said: I will give them personally, but they are not the same regiment to which my hon. friend belongs. I will make the same answer to my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson).
In the town of Louisburg there is also a Marconi cable station, and around this station there are 100 or 150 soldiers. That town is some 14 miles from Glace bay. It happens that the only men engaged in the meat business in Lewisburg are Liberals, Peters Bros., I think the name is. They wanted to sell meat to the soldiers but they could not sell to the militia because they were Liberals; and all the meat eaten by the Canadian militia at Louisburg is carried all the way from Glace bay, some 14 miles distant, and the contract was not obtained by tender. In every little house that was made for the accommodation of the soldiers in the town of Glace bay and the surrounding districts there was not a nail driven, not a door put up, by any man who was ever suspected of voting Liberal. Yet the Minister of Militia tells me there is no politics in his department! Perhaps the minister does not know it. I take this opportunity of bringing it to his attention and



telling him that it is time he did know it and that it is time this sort of thing was remedied. I believe that the Minister of Militia would remedy it, and that he is the kind of man who would abolish such methods if he knew the facts of the case.

Is my hon. friend not aware that the contract for supplying the troops quartered in Sydney was awarded to a very staunch Liberal, and that all supplies of food, meat, etc., are supplied by that Liberal contractor?
I do not know that such is the fact; I do know that the very contrary is the fact.
I can assure him that it is a fact and I can give the name.

The hon. member does not know as much about Sydney as I do, and I want to assure him that that is not the case in Sydney or elsewhere in the riding of South Cape Breton.
I believe that those things should be remedied. I bring to -the attention of the Minister of Militia also the case of a young man who has been a lieutenant in our county in the Canadian militia for some nine years. When war broke out he wanted to enlist, and desired, of course, to keep the rank to which he was entitled. Notwithstanding the fact that since the war broke out until, I think, October, at least fifty men from Cape Breton were given commissions (men who had never carried a gun or donned the uniform of a Canadian militia man), after having taken some course in Halifax, and perhaps they are good men, but this young man was unlaible to obtain a commission. Why? I do not know of any other reason except that he would not bow down to the Conservative nabob in politics in Glace Bay and go and make his application through him. Hundreds of such cases exist, but I hope the time has come when the Militia Department will do away with this method of doing business and use better judgment and tactics.

merce, a war to capture some, at least, of the business of the countries against which we are fighting, a war for commercial supremacy. I helieve it will toe captured toy the country whose resources are best fitted for the work, by the people whose technical training has not been overlooked in this time of stress. In the past German supremacy in *certain trades, and in the manufacture of certain goods was due to the fact that the national revenues had been abundantly used in the establishment and maintenance of technical institutes, trade schools, and other institutions whose chief object was to keep the national industries supplied with an army of skilled artisans. Other countries did the same to a lesser extent; England did the same, and so did the United States and Switzerland.
Some years ago there was appointed in this country a commission . to investigate technical education. This commission did splendid work, they investigated the conditions, not only in this country, but in the United States 'and Europe as well. Some two years ago they made a very voluminous report recommending certain things. During the session of 1914, in answer to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) the Minister of Labour said in connection with what the Government intended to do with that report:
The Government while having given the matter some consideration have not reached a conclusion as to what course we shall take and will not be in a position to reach Such a con-

elusion until we have heard from all the local
governments In Canada.
That was in 1914. In 1915, on page 494 of Hansard, I asked a question about technical education. The answer of the Minister of Labour was:
When the skies are clear we can make satisfactory arrangements with the provincial governments to render material assistance in respect to technical education.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that when the skies are clear, it may ibe too late in this country to give the required assistance to technical education. Last year my hon. friend the Minister of Labour replied to a question concerning the i jurisdiction of this Parliament in that matter. I do not see how the question of jurisdiction affects the matter at all.
